Conclusion applies under the stated regularity and fixed-interval setting.

accepted_variants: Local order p+1 and global order p under the unnormalized-defect convention.
cards.definition: For a stable order-p method over a fixed interval, an unnormalized per-step defect O(h^(p+1)) typically accumulates over O(1/h) steps into global error O(h^p). This uses smoothness and controlled error amplification.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an O(h squared) one-step defect makes Euler globally second-order.
cards.prompt: What is Local versus Global Error Order? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One-step defect typically has one extra power of h.
Global estimate needs stability and a fixed time range.

accepted_variants: Gronwall controls accumulation and amplification of numerical defects.
cards.definition: A Gronwall estimate bounds numerical error recurrences or inequalities by accumulated local forcing times an exponential amplification factor. It connects local defects with finite-time global-error control when the field is Lipschitz.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the estimate prevents all long-time exponential separation.
cards.prompt: What is Gronwall and Numerical Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Bounds propagated error using an integral or discrete inequality.
Amplification depends on a Lipschitz-type bound.

accepted_variants: A derivative-based linear map on functions.
cards.definition: A linear differential operator maps x to a linear combination of its derivatives, Lx = sum a_k(t)x^(k). It obeys L(alpha u + beta v) = alpha Lu + beta Lv.
major_error_concepts: Including products such as x x' in a linear operator.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Differential Operator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Linear combination of derivatives with time-dependent coefficients.
Preserves linear combinations.

cards.definition: A homogeneous linear ODE has the form Lx = 0. Its solutions form a vector space, unlike the solution set of a general nonzero-forcing equation.
major_error_concepts: Confusing linear homogeneity with a nonlinear ratio-dependent homogeneous-type equation.
cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Linear Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero right-hand side for a linear operator.
Solution set closed under linear combinations.

cards.definition: A nonhomogeneous linear ODE has the form Lx = g with specified forcing g not identically zero. Its solutions differ from each other by solutions of the associated homogeneous equation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a sum of two solutions to the same nonzero-forcing equation solves that same equation.
cards.prompt: What is Nonhomogeneous Linear Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Specified nonzero forcing.
Differences of solutions satisfy Lx = 0.

cards.definition: A fundamental set for a regular nth-order homogeneous linear ODE consists of n linearly independent solutions spanning its solution space on the interval. Every homogeneous solution is their constant-coefficient linear combination.
major_error_concepts: Using dependent solutions as a fundamental set.
cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Set of Solutions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: n independent solutions for an order-n regular equation.
They span the homogeneous solution space.

accepted_variants: No function lies in the constant linear span of the others.
cards.definition: Functions are linearly independent on an interval when a constant-coefficient combination vanishes identically only if every coefficient is zero. Dependence concerns equality over the interval, not at just one point.
major_error_concepts: Declaring functions dependent because they share a zero at one point.
cards.prompt: What is Linear Independence of Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Only the trivial constant-coefficient combination is identically zero.

accepted_variants: A derivative determinant testing a candidate fundamental family.
cards.definition: The Wronskian of n functions is the determinant with columns containing each function and its derivatives through order n-1. A nonzero value proves independence; stronger zero-versus-nonzero conclusions require additional assumptions, such as a common regular linear ODE.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an identically zero Wronskian proves dependence for every arbitrary differentiable family.
cards.prompt: What is Wronskian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Determinant of functions and successive derivatives.
Nonzero Wronskian implies independence; zero alone is subtler for arbitrary functions.

cards.definition: The complementary solution is the general solution of the homogeneous equation associated with a nonhomogeneous linear ODE. Adding a particular solution yields the full nonhomogeneous family.
major_error_concepts: Calling one forced solution the complementary solution.
cards.prompt: What is Complementary Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: General homogeneous part of the solution.

accepted_variants: One representative in the affine nonhomogeneous solution set.
cards.definition: A particular solution is one specified function satisfying a nonhomogeneous linear equation. It contains no requirement to span all solutions; different choices differ by a homogeneous solution.
major_error_concepts: Demanding that a particular solution alone satisfy every possible initial condition.
cards.prompt: What is Particular Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One solution of the forced equation.
Not the whole general family.

cards.definition: For a linear operator, homogeneous solutions can be combined with constant coefficients to produce another homogeneous solution. More generally, combining solutions with different forcings combines the forcings by the same coefficients.
major_error_concepts: Applying unrestricted solution superposition to nonlinear equations.
cards.prompt: What is Superposition Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Linearity carries combinations of solutions to combinations of forcing.
Same zero forcing is preserved in the homogeneous case.

accepted_variants: Construct a second solution from a known first one.
cards.definition: Reduction of order uses a known nonzero solution y1 of a second-order homogeneous linear equation and seeks another as y = v y1. Substitution reduces the remaining task to an equation of lower order on intervals where the construction is valid.
major_error_concepts: Treating the multiplier v as necessarily constant.
cards.prompt: What is Reduction of Order? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Use y = v y1 with one known solution.
Reduces order on an appropriate interval.

accepted_variants: Variation of constants in a homogeneous solution basis.
cards.definition: Variation of parameters seeks a forced linear solution as a combination of homogeneous basis solutions with time-dependent coefficients. Auxiliary conditions give equations for those coefficient derivatives and hence a particular solution.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the variable coefficients are arbitrary after the forcing equation is imposed.
cards.prompt: What is Variation of Parameters? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Replace constant homogeneous coefficients by functions.
Use a fundamental family to construct a forced response.

accepted_variants: n independent initial data parameterize the homogeneous solution space.
cards.definition: A regular nth-order homogeneous linear scalar ODE has an n-dimensional solution space on its interval. The standard assumptions include continuous normalized coefficients and a nonvanishing leading coefficient before normalization.
major_error_concepts: Applying the dimension statement unchanged through singular leading-coefficient zeros.
cards.prompt: What is Dimension of the Homogeneous Solution Space? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dimension equals order under regular linear-ODE hypotheses.
Leading coefficient must not vanish on the interval.
cards.term: Dimension of the Homogeneous Solution Space

accepted_variants: Affine translate of the homogeneous solution space.
cards.definition: If x_p is one solution of Lx = g, every solution is x = x_h + x_p with Lx_h = 0. This follows because subtracting two forced solutions cancels the forcing.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying a particular solution by an arbitrary constant while keeping the forcing unchanged.
cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous plus Particular Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: General solution equals homogeneous solution plus one particular solution.

accepted_variants: Characteristic-root construction of a fundamental family.
cards.definition: For a constant-coefficient homogeneous linear ODE, substituting e^(rt) gives a characteristic polynomial. A root r of multiplicity m contributes t^k e^(rt) for k from zero to m-1; complex conjugate roots combine into real exponential-sinusoidal solutions.
major_error_concepts: Using only one exponential for a repeated root and claiming a complete basis.
cards.prompt: What is Characteristic Polynomial Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Exponential ansatz leads to the characteristic polynomial.
Repeated roots require polynomial factors.

accepted_variants: Abel's identity for a second-order linear equation.
cards.definition: For y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = 0, the Wronskian satisfies W' = -pW, hence W(t) = W(t0) exp(-integral from t0 to t of p(s) ds). It is either nowhere zero or identically zero on a regular interval.
major_error_concepts: Using q rather than p in the Wronskian exponential.
cards.prompt: What is Abel's Wronskian Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Wronskian satisfies the scalar first-order equation W' = -pW.
Conclusion holds on an interval of regular coefficients.

cards.definition: A harmonic oscillator satisfies x'' + omega0 squared x = 0 with omega0 positive. Its solutions are sinusoidal combinations with constant amplitude in the ideal unforced, undamped model.
major_error_concepts: Calling every periodic nonlinear motion exactly harmonic.
cards.prompt: What is Harmonic Oscillator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Linear restoring equation with positive squared frequency.
Sinusoidal undamped free motion.

cards.definition: In m x'' + c x' + k x = 0 with m and k positive, positive c models viscous damping. The discriminant c squared - 4mk distinguishes underdamped, critically damped, and overdamped motion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming positive damping always permits oscillation.
cards.prompt: What is Oscillator Damping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Positive velocity-proportional resistance.
Damping regime depends on the characteristic roots.

cards.definition: Forcing is a prescribed external input on the right-hand side of an ODE, such as F(t) in m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t). It drives a response in addition to free homogeneous motion.
major_error_concepts: Calling initial displacement itself a continuing external force.
cards.prompt: What is Oscillator Forcing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Given external input.
Distinguish forced response from homogeneous motion.

accepted_variants: The oscillator's unforced undamped characteristic frequency.
cards.definition: The natural angular frequency of an ideal mass-spring oscillator is omega0 = sqrt(k/m). It describes undamped free motion and differs from the damped oscillation frequency when damping is present.
major_error_concepts: Equating natural frequency with any imposed drive frequency.
cards.prompt: What is Natural Frequency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Undamped free-oscillation angular frequency.
omega0 = sqrt(k/m).

cards.definition: Resonance is an enhanced response when a drive interacts with an oscillatory mode near its characteristic frequency. A sinusoidally forced undamped linear oscillator at exact resonance has secular amplitude growth; damping limits the steady-state response and can shift its peak.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every damped resonant response grows without bound.
cards.prompt: What is Resonance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Drive couples strongly near a modal frequency.
Distinguish ideal undamped growth from damped finite response.

cards.definition: Beats are slow amplitude modulations produced by superposing oscillations with nearby frequencies. For equal-amplitude cosines, the product identity separates a rapid carrier from a slow envelope associated with their frequency difference.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting beats as evidence of dissipative damping by themselves.
cards.prompt: What is Beats? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Superposition of nearby frequencies.
Slow amplitude modulation differs from the rapid oscillation.

accepted_variants: The decaying free response before long-time forced behavior dominates.
cards.definition: The transient response is the part of a solution associated with initial conditions that disappears with time in a stable dissipative linear system. In such a system it is represented by decaying homogeneous modes.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every homogeneous solution decays even in an unstable or undamped system.
cards.prompt: What is Transient Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Initial-condition contribution that decays under stability assumptions.

cards.definition: A steady-state response is the persistent long-time response to sustained forcing after decaying transients vanish. For a stable linear oscillator under sinusoidal forcing it is a sinusoid at the drive frequency with an amplitude and phase shift.
major_error_concepts: Equating steady state with zero time derivative in every forced system.
cards.prompt: What is Steady-State Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Persistent response after stable transients decay.
Need not be a constant value.

accepted_variants: High Q means relatively small fractional energy loss per oscillation.
cards.definition: For a lightly damped linear oscillator, the quality factor Q measures weak damping and sharp frequency selectivity. With m x'' + c x' + k x = 0, Q = m omega0/c; it is also approximately 2 pi times stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle in the weak-damping regime.
major_error_concepts: Claiming high Q means stronger damping.
cards.prompt: What is Quality Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dimensionless measure of damping and resonance sharpness.
State the weak-damping condition for the cycle-loss interpretation.

cards.definition: The equation m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t) balances inertia, linear viscous resistance, and linear restoring force against an external drive. Standard mechanical interpretations take m positive, k positive, and c nonnegative.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting c x' as the spring displacement force.
cards.prompt: What is Forced Damped Oscillator Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Identify inertia, damping, stiffness, and forcing terms.
State the linear model assumptions.

accepted_variants: A nonsingular analytic point of the linear equation.
cards.definition: For a normalized second-order linear equation y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0, an ordinary point is one where p and q are analytic in a neighborhood. Power-series solution theory applies there.
major_error_concepts: Calling a point ordinary without first accounting for a vanishing leading coefficient.
cards.prompt: What is Ordinary Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalized coefficients analytic near the point.

accepted_variants: A point where the equation is not ordinary in the analytic-coefficient sense.
cards.definition: A singular point of a linear ODE is a point where the normalized coefficient conditions for an ordinary point fail. It may arise from dividing by a leading coefficient that vanishes there.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every solution must diverge at every singular point.
cards.prompt: What is Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Failure of the normalized ordinary-point regularity.

accepted_variants: A singularity mild enough for the standard Frobenius framework.
cards.definition: For y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0, x0 is regular singular when (x-x0)p(x) and (x-x0) squared q(x) extend analytically near x0, even though x0 is singular. These controlled poles permit Frobenius theory.
major_error_concepts: Requiring p and q themselves to be analytic and thereby confusing regular singular with ordinary.
cards.prompt: What is Regular Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Weighted coefficients extend analytically.
Second-order weights are first and second powers respectively.

accepted_variants: A singularity outside the regular-singular class.
cards.definition: An irregular singular point is a singular point that fails the regular-singular conditions. The local solution behavior may require techniques beyond ordinary Frobenius power series, such as asymptotic expansions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the usual indicial polynomial always completely describes irregular-singular behavior.
cards.prompt: What is Irregular Singular Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Singular but not regular singular.

accepted_variants: Local analytic solution construction by a Taylor-type series.
cards.definition: A power-series solution represents the unknown as sum a_n(x-x0)^n near a point. Substituting into the ODE and matching coefficients determines recurrence relations and free coefficients corresponding to initial data.
major_error_concepts: Treating a formal recurrence as proof of convergence without suitable analytic conditions.
cards.prompt: What is Power-Series Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Series representation about a center.
Coefficient matching gives recurrence relations.

accepted_variants: The maximal open disk of power-series convergence.
cards.definition: The radius of convergence is the radius of the interval or complex disk where a power series converges absolutely about its center. For analytic ODE solutions, singularities of the normalized equation constrain the region guaranteed by local analytic theory, though individual solutions may extend farther.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every coefficient singularity must be a singularity of every solution.
cards.prompt: What is Radius of Convergence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Convergence distance from the expansion center.
Distinguish guaranteed coefficient-domain bounds from a particular solution's possible extension.

accepted_variants: Generalized power-series construction at a regular singular point.
cards.definition: The Frobenius method seeks y = (x-x0)^r sum a_n(x-x0)^n near a regular singular point, with a0 nonzero. The exponent is selected by an indicial equation; a second independent solution may require logarithmic terms.
major_error_concepts: Guaranteeing two plain Frobenius series for every pair of indicial roots.
cards.prompt: What is Frobenius Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Power factor times analytic series.
Indicial exponents and possible logarithmic companion solution.

accepted_variants: The characteristic equation for Frobenius exponents.
cards.definition: The indicial equation is the algebraic condition on the leading exponent r obtained from the lowest-power term of a Frobenius substitution. Its roots guide the possible local solution forms near a regular singular point.
major_error_concepts: Confusing it with the constant-coefficient characteristic polynomial in all cases.
cards.prompt: What is Indicial Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Lowest-order balance determines the exponent.
Root relations influence companion solution form.

accepted_variants: Ordinary-point analytic existence for linear equations.
cards.definition: At an ordinary point of a linear ODE with analytic normalized coefficients, the IVP has a local analytic solution represented by a convergent power series. The required initial values determine the free series coefficients.
major_error_concepts: Claiming smooth but nonanalytic coefficients automatically yield convergent Taylor solutions.
cards.prompt: What is Ordinary-Point Series Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Analytic normalized coefficients yield local analytic solutions.
Initial data determine the appropriate coefficients.

cards.definition: At a regular singular point, Frobenius theory provides local solution forms based on indicial exponents. Depending on repeated roots or integer root differences, a second solution can involve logarithms rather than another independent plain power-factor series.
major_error_concepts: Discarding a logarithmic solution simply because it is not a pure power series.
cards.prompt: What is Regular-Singular Solution Forms? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regular singularity permits Frobenius-type construction.
Logarithmic terms may be needed.

cards.definition: Standard differential equations define named solution families, such as Bessel, Airy, and Legendre functions. They extend the useful library beyond elementary formulas, but a special function need not be non-elementary: for certain parameters, Legendre solutions include polynomials. Boundary conditions and normalization determine which member or combination solves a particular problem.
major_error_concepts: No Legendre polynomial can count as a special function because it has an elementary polynomial expression.
cards.prompt: What role do special-function families play as ODE solutions, and must every member be non-elementary?
required_concepts: Named solution families arise from standard ODEs.
Special-function status does not imply every member is non-elementary.
Parameters and boundary or normalization conditions matter.

cards.definition: A first-order system x' = f(t,x) evolves a vector of state variables whose derivatives may depend on one another. A higher-order scalar ODE can be rewritten as such a system by including lower derivatives in the state.
major_error_concepts: Treating coupled coordinates as independent scalar IVPs without their coupling terms.
cards.prompt: What is First-Order ODE System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector-valued first-order evolution.
Higher-order equations can be converted to first-order systems.

cards.definition: A linear first-order system has the form x' = A(t)x + g(t), with a time-dependent matrix A and prescribed forcing vector g. Linearity concerns state dependence, not whether A is constant.
major_error_concepts: Calling a system nonlinear solely because its matrix varies with time.
cards.prompt: What is Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Matrix-linear state dependence plus prescribed forcing.

cards.definition: A homogeneous linear system is x' = A(t)x with zero forcing. Its solution set is a vector space and a fundamental matrix can propagate any initial state.
major_error_concepts: Calling a system homogeneous merely because its matrix is constant.
cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero forcing in a linear system.

cards.definition: An inhomogeneous linear system is x' = A(t)x + g(t) with a prescribed nonzero forcing vector. Its general solution consists of a homogeneous solution plus any one particular solution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a linear combination of same-forcing solutions retains that same forcing without coefficient restrictions.
cards.prompt: What is Inhomogeneous Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonzero prescribed forcing vector.
Homogeneous-plus-particular structure.

cards.definition: A fundamental matrix Phi(t) has linearly independent homogeneous solution vectors as its columns. It satisfies Phi' = A(t)Phi and is invertible throughout a regular solution interval.
major_error_concepts: Calling any singular collection of solution columns a fundamental matrix.
cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent solution columns.
Invertible matrix satisfying the homogeneous matrix equation.

accepted_variants: The exponential propagator for a constant linear system.
cards.definition: The matrix exponential exp(At) is defined by the convergent series sum (At)^k/k!. For constant A it satisfies d exp(At)/dt = A exp(At) and exp(A0) = I, including when A is not diagonalizable.
major_error_concepts: Exponentiating each matrix entry independently and calling that the matrix exponential.
cards.prompt: What is Matrix Exponential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Series definition and constant-matrix evolution property.
Does not require diagonalizability.

cards.definition: Variation of constants for x' = A(t)x + g(t) uses a fundamental matrix Phi to give x(t) = Phi(t)[Phi(t0)^-1 x0 + integral from t0 to t of Phi(s)^-1 g(s) ds]. It separates homogeneous propagation from accumulated forcing.
major_error_concepts: Removing the inverse fundamental matrix from the forcing integral without justification.
cards.prompt: What is Variation of Constants? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Fundamental matrix propagates both initial data and transformed forcing.
Inverse matrix acts at the integration time inside the integral.

accepted_variants: Generalized eigenvectors describe non-diagonalizable linear evolution.
cards.definition: A Jordan-form viewpoint decomposes constant-matrix dynamics into eigenvalue growth or decay together with polynomial factors from nilpotent Jordan blocks. A size-m block can generate powers through t^(m-1) multiplying an exponential.
major_error_concepts: Dropping all polynomial factors when a matrix has a nontrivial Jordan block.
cards.prompt: What is Jordan Blocks and Linear Dynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Eigenvalue exponentials plus polynomial factors for defective blocks.
Diagonalization is not always possible.

cards.definition: For x' = Ax with constant matrix A and x(t0) = x0, the solution is x(t) = exp(A(t-t0))x0. The formula handles coupled coordinates and does not require A to be diagonalizable.
major_error_concepts: Using exp(At)x0 while ignoring a nonzero initial time.
cards.prompt: What is Homogeneous Matrix-Exponential Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Constant A and the time difference t-t0.
Multiply the initial vector by the matrix exponential.

accepted_variants: Duhamel or variation-of-constants formula for constant A.
cards.definition: For constant A, the forced solution is x(t) = exp(A(t-t0))x0 + integral from t0 to t of exp(A(t-s))g(s) ds. Each forcing contribution is propagated from its application time s to the observation time t.
major_error_concepts: Replacing exp(A(t-s)) by exp(At) inside the integral in general.
cards.prompt: What is Forced Matrix-Exponential Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Initial propagation plus convolution-type forcing integral.
Kernel depends on t-s.

accepted_variants: State-space picture of a dynamical system.
cards.definition: A phase portrait depicts solution trajectories in state space for an autonomous system, often together with equilibria and direction arrows. It displays geometric evolution rather than plotting every state coordinate against time.
major_error_concepts: Reading a closed orbit as a constant equilibrium merely because it closes in space.
cards.prompt: What is Phase Portrait? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Trajectories in phase space.
Direction and qualitative structures characterize dynamics.

accepted_variants: A zero-component curve of the planar field.
cards.definition: A nullcline is a set where one component of a planar vector field vanishes. On an x-nullcline x' = 0 but y' may be nonzero; intersections of all component nullclines are equilibrium candidates.
major_error_concepts: Calling every point of one nullcline a full equilibrium.
cards.prompt: What is Nullcline? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One derivative component vanishes.
A single nullcline need not consist of equilibria.

accepted_variants: A set preserved by the flow.
cards.definition: A set is positively invariant if trajectories starting in it remain there for forward time. Full invariance includes both forward and backward evolution wherever the flow is defined.
major_error_concepts: Equating forward invariance with two-sided invariance without additional assumptions.
cards.prompt: What is Invariant Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: State the time direction of invariance.
Trajectories do not leave the set in that direction.

accepted_variants: The flow path through an initial state.
cards.definition: A trajectory or orbit is the set traced in phase space by a solution as time varies. The parameterized solution includes timing information that the geometric orbit alone may omit.
major_error_concepts: Assuming identical geometric orbits always imply identical speeds along them.
cards.prompt: What is Trajectory? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: State-space path generated by a solution.
Distinguish geometry from time parameterization.

accepted_variants: The set of possible long-time accumulation states.
cards.definition: The omega-limit set of a forward trajectory consists of state-space limit points reached along sequences of times tending to infinity. For a precompact trajectory in a regular flow, it is nonempty and compact.
major_error_concepts: Defining it as the set of all states visited at any finite time.
cards.prompt: What is Omega-Limit Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Accumulation points along times going to positive infinity.
Nonemptiness needs conditions such as precompactness.

accepted_variants: A set approached by nearby or otherwise specified forward trajectories.
cards.definition: An attractor is an invariant set that attracts a specified neighborhood or class of initial states under the adopted definition. Attractors may be equilibria, periodic orbits, or more complicated sets; stability and minimality conventions should be stated when needed.
major_error_concepts: Calling any one point temporarily approached by a trajectory an attractor.
cards.prompt: What is Attractor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Invariant attracting set.
Need not be a single point.

cards.definition: A repeller is an invariant set that attracts nearby trajectories under reversed time in the appropriate local setting, or equivalently repels them forward under corresponding assumptions. It is not merely any equilibrium with one unstable direction.
major_error_concepts: Equating every unstable equilibrium with a full repeller.
cards.prompt: What is Repeller? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Invariant set with backward attraction or suitable forward repulsion.
A saddle need not be a repeller.

cards.definition: A trapping region is a region that forward trajectories cannot leave, often established by a vector field pointing strictly inward on its boundary. A compact trapping region can confine long-time dynamics without identifying a unique attractor.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every trapping region contains exactly one equilibrium.
cards.prompt: What is Trapping Region? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Forward confinement.
Inward boundary direction is a common sufficient condition.

cards.definition: A planar vector field assigns a velocity vector f(x,y) to each point of a two-dimensional state domain. Its integral curves satisfy x' = f1(x,y), y' = f2(x,y).
major_error_concepts: Interpreting the vector field as a position vector rather than the state's derivative.
cards.prompt: What is Planar Vector Field? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: A velocity vector assigned at each planar state.
Integral curves follow those assigned directions.

accepted_variants: Persistent closeness under small initial perturbations.
cards.definition: Lyapunov stability of an equilibrium means every sufficiently small permitted error in initial state remains small for all future time. Formally, each epsilon neighborhood has a delta neighborhood whose trajectories stay inside it.
major_error_concepts: Requiring nearby trajectories to converge in order to satisfy stability alone.
cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Epsilon-delta forward-time closeness.
Convergence is not required.

accepted_variants: A stable equilibrium with local asymptotic convergence.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is asymptotically stable when it is Lyapunov stable and nearby forward trajectories converge to it. The neighborhood of attraction can be local rather than all phase space.
major_error_concepts: Calling an equilibrium globally attracting based only on a local theorem.
cards.prompt: What is Asymptotic Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Stability and attraction together.
Local need not mean global.

accepted_variants: Stability with a controlled exponential convergence rate.
cards.definition: An equilibrium is exponentially stable when nearby deviations obey a bound |x(t)-x_star| <= C exp(-alpha(t-t0))|x0-x_star| with positive C and alpha. This provides a quantitative decay rate stronger than asymptotic stability alone.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every asymptotically stable equilibrium converges exponentially.
cards.prompt: What is Exponential Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Uniform local exponential decay bound.
Stronger than merely tending to zero.

accepted_variants: First-order Taylor approximation of the vector field at equilibrium.
cards.definition: Linearization approximates a differentiable autonomous system near equilibrium x_star by u' = Df(x_star)u for the small displacement u = x-x_star. Nonlinear remainder terms are higher order, but can matter when the linear part is inconclusive.
major_error_concepts: Treating the linearized model as a globally exact system.
cards.prompt: What is Linearization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Jacobian gives the first-order local dynamics.
Zero-real-part eigenvalues can require nonlinear analysis.

accepted_variants: The derivative matrix of the vector field.
cards.definition: The Jacobian matrix Df(x_star) has entries partial f_i/partial x_j evaluated at the equilibrium. It records how each derivative component responds to small state perturbations.
major_error_concepts: Using partial derivatives with respect to time in place of state derivatives for an autonomous Jacobian.
cards.prompt: What is Jacobian at Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Matrix of first state partial derivatives at the specified point.

accepted_variants: An energy-like stability certificate without explicit integration.
cards.definition: A Lyapunov function is a scalar function used to assess stability by its value and derivative along trajectories. Near an equilibrium, a positive-definite V with nonpositive trajectory derivative is a standard sufficient structure for stability.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any scalar function with a local minimum proves stability without checking its derivative along the flow.
cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Scalar measure positive away from equilibrium.
Derivative along solutions controls whether it decreases.

accepted_variants: A differential relation bounding possible evolution.
cards.definition: A differential inequality bounds a derivative rather than specifying it exactly, such as u' <= a(t)u+b(t). Comparison arguments turn such bounds into estimates on solutions, growth, or perturbations.
major_error_concepts: Replacing an inequality by equality and claiming the resulting comparison function is the original solution.
cards.prompt: What is Differential Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Derivative inequality used for comparison bounds.

accepted_variants: An exponential comparison estimate for an integral growth inequality.
cards.definition: A basic Gronwall inequality states that if nonnegative u satisfies u(t) <= a + integral from t0 to t of b(s)u(s) ds, with a nonnegative and b nonnegative integrable, then u(t) <= a exp(integral b). It bounds accumulated feedback growth.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion without accounting for the sign and integrability assumptions.
cards.prompt: What is Gronwall Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Integral inequality with nonnegative data.
Exponential upper bound.

cards.definition: For a continuously differentiable system near equilibrium, strictly negative real parts of all Jacobian eigenvalues imply local exponential stability. A positive-real-part eigenvalue implies instability; zero real parts make this test inconclusive in general.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a nonlinear equilibrium stable solely because all real parts are nonpositive.
cards.prompt: What is Jacobian Eigenvalue Stability Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative real parts imply local stability; a positive real part implies instability.
Zero-real-part cases need more analysis.

accepted_variants: Stability analysis by a decreasing energy-like function.
cards.definition: The Lyapunov direct method proves stability using a positive-definite scalar V and its trajectory derivative Vdot = gradient V dot f. Nonpositive Vdot gives stability under standard local assumptions; negative-definite Vdot gives asymptotic stability with the appropriate neighborhood conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Vdot <= 0 alone always gives asymptotic convergence without an additional argument.
cards.prompt: What is Lyapunov Direct Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inspect V and its derivative along the actual vector field.
Distinguish nonpositive from negative-definite derivative conclusions.

accepted_variants: Quantitative finite-time dependence on equation parameters.
cards.definition: Parameter sensitivity estimates bound differences between solutions of nearby parameterized equations. Under state-Lipschitz and controlled parameter dependence, a Gronwall argument bounds finite-time solution differences by initial mismatch and parameter-induced forcing differences.
major_error_concepts: Inferring uniform infinite-time sensitivity control from a finite-interval estimate.
cards.prompt: What is Parameter Sensitivity Estimate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compare two parameterized solutions on a common interval.
Include parameter forcing difference and error amplification.

cards.definition: If f is L-Lipschitz in state on the relevant region, two solutions of the same equation satisfy |x(t)-y(t)| <= exp(L(t-t0))|x0-y0| over their common forward interval. This controls finite-time dependence without asserting contraction.
major_error_concepts: Treating the upper bound as an exact equality for every pair of solutions.
cards.prompt: What is Initial-Data Sensitivity Estimate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Initial separation multiplied by an exponential bound.
Positive L bound need not imply solutions actually diverge.

accepted_variants: Local qualitative dynamics match the hyperbolic linearization.
cards.definition: The Hartman-Grobman theorem states that near a hyperbolic equilibrium of a sufficiently regular finite-dimensional autonomous system, the nonlinear flow is locally topologically conjugate to its linearization. Hyperbolic means no Jacobian eigenvalue has zero real part; the correspondence need not be differentiable.
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem at a center with purely imaginary eigenvalues.
cards.prompt: What is Hartman–Grobman Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Hyperbolic equilibrium requirement.
Local topological equivalence, not exact equality of nonlinear and linear solutions.

accepted_variants: A closed orbit of the flow.
cards.definition: A periodic orbit is the phase-space path of a nonconstant solution satisfying x(t+T) = x(t) for some positive T. The same closed geometric path is traversed repeatedly.
major_error_concepts: Counting an equilibrium as a nontrivial periodic orbit merely because its constant solution repeats.
cards.prompt: What is Periodic Orbit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonconstant solution repeating after a positive period.

cards.definition: A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit: sufficiently nearby periodic orbits do not form a continuous family around it. It may be attracting, repelling, or have one-sided stability.
major_error_concepts: Calling every closed orbit around a linear center a limit cycle.
cards.prompt: What is Limit Cycle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Periodic orbit isolated among periodic orbits.
Need not be attracting.

accepted_variants: A bounded planar long-time limit without equilibria must be a closed orbit in the standard setting.
cards.definition: A standard Poincare-Bendixson result says that for a continuously differentiable planar autonomous flow, a nonempty compact omega-limit set containing no equilibria is a periodic orbit under the usual planar hypotheses. It is a special restriction of two-dimensional flows, not a general higher-dimensional theorem.
major_error_concepts: Applying the result unchanged to three-dimensional chaotic systems.
cards.prompt: What is Poincare–Bendixson Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Planar autonomous setting with compact omega-limit set.
No equilibria in that set leads to a periodic orbit.

accepted_variants: A one-sign divergence test excluding closed orbits.
cards.definition: The Bendixson-Dulac criterion rules out periodic orbits in a simply connected planar region when a suitable continuously differentiable multiplier B makes divergence of Bf strictly one sign throughout that region. It is a nonexistence criterion, not a recipe locating a cycle.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a periodic orbit exists whenever the criterion fails.
cards.prompt: What is Bendixson–Dulac Criterion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Signed divergence of a Dulac-weighted planar field.
Simply connected domain and regularity conditions.

cards.definition: A two-point boundary value problem imposes conditions at both ends of an interval, such as y(a)=alpha and y(b)=beta. Solvability depends on the equation, interval, and boundary operator, not just the number of conditions.
major_error_concepts: Applying an IVP uniqueness theorem directly to conclude every two-point BVP is uniquely solvable.
cards.prompt: What is Two-Point Boundary Value Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Data at two distinct endpoints.
Existence and uniqueness require separate analysis.

accepted_variants: The integral kernel of the linear boundary operator's inverse.
cards.definition: A Green's function represents the response of a linear differential boundary problem to a point source while satisfying its boundary conditions. When the inverse exists, integrating G(x,s) against the forcing constructs the corresponding solution, with conventions set by the operator.
major_error_concepts: Using a Green's function for one boundary condition unchanged for an incompatible boundary condition.
cards.prompt: What is Green's Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Impulse response for a specified linear operator and boundary conditions.
Integral representation requires appropriate solvability.

accepted_variants: A symmetric differential expression realized with an appropriate self-adjoint domain.
cards.definition: A self-adjoint differential operator equals its adjoint under a specified inner product and operator domain. Integration by parts and boundary conditions are essential; formal symmetry of the differential expression alone does not determine a self-adjoint boundary problem.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring boundary terms and declaring any formally symmetric expression self-adjoint on every domain.
cards.prompt: What is Self-Adjoint Operator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equality to adjoint includes inner product and domain.
Boundary conditions matter.

cards.definition: An eigenvalue problem seeks scalars lambda and nonzero functions y satisfying Ly = lambda w y with specified boundary conditions. Boundary conditions restrict the permitted values and distinguish it from an unconstrained forced equation.
major_error_concepts: Accepting the zero function as an eigenfunction for every lambda.
cards.prompt: What is Differential Eigenvalue Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonzero eigenfunction and spectral parameter.
Boundary conditions are part of the problem.

accepted_variants: A self-adjoint second-order boundary spectral problem.
cards.definition: A Sturm-Liouville problem has the form -(p y')' + q y = lambda w y with suitable boundary conditions. In the regular self-adjoint case on a finite interval, p and w are positive and the theory gives real eigenvalues and weighted orthogonality.
major_error_concepts: Claiming arbitrary non-self-adjoint boundary conditions preserve all Sturm-Liouville conclusions.
cards.prompt: What is Sturm–Liouville Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Self-adjoint second-order weighted eigenvalue form.
State regularity, positivity, and boundary assumptions for the spectral conclusions.

cards.definition: Eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint Sturm-Liouville problem with distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal in the weighted inner product: integral w y_m y_n = 0 in the real case. The weight is part of the problem and cannot generally be omitted.
major_error_concepts: Claiming unweighted orthogonality when the problem has a nonconstant weight.
cards.prompt: What is Eigenfunction Orthogonality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distinct eigenvalues imply weighted orthogonality.
Use the specified weight and self-adjoint boundary setting.

accepted_variants: Boundary solvability is a global constraint issue.
cards.definition: Regular IVPs select a solution from data at one point, whereas BVPs impose constraints across an interval. Even a smooth linear equation can have no BVP solution or infinitely many at special parameters despite well-behaved IVP uniqueness.
major_error_concepts: Using a successful IVP uniqueness result as proof that all boundary data are compatible.
cards.prompt: What is IVP–BVP Distinction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Local initial data and distributed boundary constraints differ.
BVP nonuniqueness can occur without IVP nonuniqueness.

accepted_variants: ODE spectral modes underpin Fourier-type and PDE expansions.
cards.definition: Sturm-Liouville eigenfunctions provide mode bases for expansions used in Fourier analysis and separation-of-variables PDE methods. Orthogonality and appropriate completeness results permit projection onto modes under the relevant function-space assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every family of independent ODE solutions automatically forms a complete orthogonal basis.
cards.prompt: What is Spectral Modes and Function Expansions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Boundary eigenfunctions supply expansion modes.
Completeness and admissible function space require stated hypotheses.

accepted_variants: Phase-space dynamics generated by a Hamiltonian function.
cards.definition: A canonical Hamiltonian system satisfies q' = partial H/partial p and p' = -partial H/partial q. When H has no explicit time dependence, H is conserved along solutions under the usual differentiability assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Reversing one canonical sign or assuming explicitly time-dependent H must remain constant.
cards.prompt: What is Hamiltonian System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Canonical paired equations with opposite sign.
Autonomous Hamiltonian is conserved.

cards.definition: A gradient system has form x' = -gradient V(x). Along its solutions, dV/dt = -|gradient V| squared <= 0, so V decreases except at critical points in the standard Euclidean setting.
major_error_concepts: Claiming V increases under negative-gradient flow.
cards.prompt: What is Gradient System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Motion follows the negative gradient.
Potential is nonincreasing along trajectories.

accepted_variants: A first integral of the differential system.
cards.definition: A conserved quantity I(x) is constant along solutions, so gradient I dot f = 0 for an autonomous differentiable system. Its level sets constrain trajectories without necessarily determining them completely.
major_error_concepts: Calling a decreasing Lyapunov function a conserved quantity.
cards.prompt: What is Conserved Quantity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Zero derivative along the flow.
Conservation restricts trajectories to level sets.

accepted_variants: Dynamics with a stated loss or contraction property.
cards.definition: A dissipative flow in the energy sense loses a specified energy-like quantity along trajectories. Other uses describe phase-volume contraction or existence of an absorbing set; these definitions are related in some models but should not be treated as universally equivalent.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a specific energy law solely from negative divergence without defining that energy.
cards.prompt: What is Dissipative Flow? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Specify the intended meaning of dissipation.
Energy decay and phase-volume contraction are distinct notions.

accepted_variants: A driven or undriven cubic-stiffness oscillator.
cards.definition: The Duffing oscillator is a nonlinear oscillator commonly written x'' + delta x' + alpha x + beta x cubed = gamma cos(omega t). The cubic restoring term permits amplitude-dependent behavior beyond the linear oscillator, with qualitative dynamics depending on parameters.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every Duffing parameter choice is chaotic.
cards.prompt: What is Duffing Oscillator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cubic nonlinear restoring term.
Damping and periodic forcing are optional model components.

cards.definition: A forced pendulum retains the nonlinear restoring term sin theta and adds external drive, often with damping: theta'' + c theta' + (g/L)sin theta = A cos(omega t). Large-angle and driven behavior can differ substantially from a linear small-angle oscillator.
major_error_concepts: Replacing sin theta by theta at arbitrary amplitude without an approximation statement.
cards.prompt: What is Forced Pendulum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonlinear sine restoring term with external forcing.
Small-angle linearization is a restricted approximation.

cards.definition: The Lorenz system is x' = sigma(y-x), y' = x(rho-z)-y, z' = xy-beta z. It is a three-dimensional autonomous nonlinear model that can exhibit chaotic dynamics for suitable parameters; chaos is not present for every parameter choice.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all three-dimensional ODEs or all Lorenz parameters are chaotic.
cards.prompt: What is Lorenz System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Three coupled autonomous nonlinear equations.
Chaotic behavior is parameter-dependent.

accepted_variants: Nonlinear counterparts of stable and unstable linear subspaces.
cards.definition: Near a hyperbolic equilibrium, stable and unstable invariant manifolds consist locally of states approaching the equilibrium in forward and backward time respectively. Their tangent spaces at the equilibrium are the stable and unstable eigenspaces of the linearization.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the nonlinear manifolds are globally identical to the linear eigenspaces.
cards.prompt: What is Stable and Unstable Manifolds? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Invariant sets of forward or backward convergence.
Tangency to corresponding linearized eigenspaces under hyperbolicity.

cards.definition: A Hopf bifurcation is a local transition in which a complex-conjugate eigenvalue pair crosses the imaginary axis and a small periodic orbit is created or destroyed under nondegeneracy and transversality conditions. The resulting cycle's stability depends on whether the bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a Hopf bifurcation from any purely imaginary eigenvalues without checking crossing and nondegeneracy.
cards.prompt: What is Hopf Bifurcation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Complex eigenvalue pair crosses zero real part.
Periodic-orbit birth or death requires the relevant nondegeneracy conditions.

cards.definition: A saddle-node bifurcation creates or destroys a pair of equilibria as a parameter crosses a threshold. The scalar normal form x' = mu - x squared has two equilibria for mu positive, one degenerate equilibrium at zero, and none for mu negative.
major_error_concepts: Calling the appearance of a periodic orbit a saddle-node bifurcation of equilibria.
cards.prompt: What is Saddle–Node Bifurcation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Collision or creation of two equilibria.
A zero eigenvalue occurs at the generic threshold.

catalog.description: Solve and interpret first- and higher-order differential equations, linear systems, phase portraits, stability, transforms, series methods, and numerical approximations.
catalog.subject: Mathematics
catalog.title: Ordinary Differential Equations

cards.definition: Organic chemistry studies the structures, properties, and transformations of carbon compounds within conventional disciplinary boundaries. Carbon's bonding versatility supports many functional groups and stereochemical arrangements; not every carbon-containing compound is treated primarily as organic chemistry.
major_error_concepts: Defining every carbon-containing material as necessarily an organic molecule.
cards.prompt: What is Organic Chemistry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Study of carbon-based molecular structure and reactivity with conventional boundaries.

cards.definition: A bond-line drawing represents carbon atoms at unlabeled line ends and vertices, with carbon-bound hydrogens usually inferred from valence. Heteroatoms, relevant hydrogens on them, charges, and stereochemical marks must be interpreted explicitly rather than silently treated as carbons.
major_error_concepts: Counting an unlabeled bend as empty space rather than a carbon atom.
cards.prompt: What is Bond Line Structure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unlabeled endpoints and corners represent carbon; implied hydrogens follow valence.

cards.definition: Constitutional isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity. They differ from conformers or stereoisomers, which preserve the bonded-atom connection pattern.
major_error_concepts: Calling two rotated drawings with identical connectivity constitutional isomers.
cards.prompt: What is Constitutional Isomer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Same formula, different connectivity.

cards.definition: A functional group is a recurring atom-and-bond arrangement associated with characteristic chemical behavior. The surrounding structure modifies that behavior, so identifying the group is a starting point rather than a complete prediction of every reaction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every molecule containing the same group has identical reaction rates and properties.
cards.prompt: What is Functional Group? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Recurring structural unit associated with characteristic reactivity.

cards.definition: Formal charge assigns bonding electrons equally between bonded atoms and compares assigned electrons with the neutral atom's valence count. It is an electron-bookkeeping quantity, not the atom's measured partial charge or oxidation state.
major_error_concepts: Equating formal charge with the actual distribution of electron density.
cards.prompt: What is Formal Charge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Valence count minus assigned nonbonding and half-bonding electrons.

cards.definition: Resonance contributors differ in electron placement while preserving nuclear positions and connectivity. The molecule is represented by a delocalized electronic structure, not by rapid physical switching between independently existing contributor molecules.
major_error_concepts: Moving atoms to create a resonance contributor or treating contributors as equilibrating isomers.
cards.prompt: What is Resonance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Electron-only alternative contributors describe one delocalized structure.

cards.definition: The octet rule is a useful valence-shell guideline for many second-row main-group atoms. Charged, electron-deficient, and radical intermediates can have incomplete octets, while ordinary second-row carbon cannot be assigned arbitrary expanded-octet bonding in a valid Lewis structure.
major_error_concepts: Drawing neutral carbon with five ordinary two-electron bonds without addressing invalid electron count.
cards.prompt: What is Octet Rule in Organic Structures? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Second-row valence counting constrains plausible organic structures.

accepted_variants: sp3, sp2, or sp hybrid-orbital model.
cards.definition: Hybridization is a localized orbital model combining atomic orbitals into directionally useful bonding orbitals. sp3, sp2, and sp descriptions often correspond to tetrahedral, trigonal-planar, and linear bonding arrangements, while remaining p orbitals can form pi systems.
major_error_concepts: Treating hybridization labels as a literal observable switching event independent of molecular bonding.
cards.prompt: What is Carbon Hybridization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Localized orbital combinations relate to bonding geometry and available p orbitals.

cards.definition: A sigma bond has bonding overlap oriented along the internuclear axis. A single bond is ordinarily a sigma bond, while double and triple bonds each contain one sigma component plus additional pi components.
major_error_concepts: Counting both components of a double bond as sigma bonds.
cards.prompt: What is Sigma Bond? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Axial bonding overlap; one sigma component per bonded atom pair in ordinary multiple bonds.

cards.definition: A pi bond arises from lateral orbital overlap with electron density on opposite sides of the internuclear axis. Maintaining parallel overlap restricts rotation, which helps make alkene stereochemistry distinct from ordinary single-bond conformations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a double bond rotates freely while preserving the same pi overlap.
cards.prompt: What is Pi Bond? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sideways overlap produces pi bonding and restricts free rotation.

accepted_variants: Tetrahedral, trigonal-planar, or linear local geometry as appropriate.
cards.definition: Local molecular geometry describes the spatial arrangement of bonded atoms around a center. Electron-pair arrangements, multiple bonding, and lone pairs influence angles, so a hybridization label is an approximation rather than an exact prediction of every bond angle.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every angle near an sp3 center is exactly the ideal tetrahedral angle.
cards.prompt: What is Organic Molecular Geometry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Three-dimensional local atom arrangement with electronic influences.

cards.definition: Bond polarity reflects unequal sharing of electron density between bonded atoms. Molecular polarity depends on the vector combination of bond dipoles and geometry, so polar bonds do not guarantee a nonzero total molecular dipole.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any molecule with a polar bond must have a net dipole.
cards.prompt: What is Bond and Molecular Polarity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unequal bond electron sharing differs from whole-molecule dipole.

cards.definition: Intermolecular forces include dispersion, dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding among molecules. They influence physical properties and differ from the intramolecular covalent bonds that determine atom connectivity.
major_error_concepts: Explaining ordinary boiling as breaking the molecule's carbon-carbon covalent skeleton.
cards.prompt: What is Organic Intermolecular Forces? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Attractions between molecules influence bulk properties.

cards.definition: Hydrogen bonding involves an appropriately polarized donor bond and a suitable acceptor electron pair. A molecule can be a donor, acceptor, both, or neither depending on structure; not every atom with a lone pair has equal acceptor ability.
major_error_concepts: Treating every hydrogen attached to carbon as equivalent to a typical O-H hydrogen-bond donor.
cards.prompt: What is Hydrogen Bond Donor and Acceptor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Specific donor-acceptor interaction depends on electronic structure.

cards.definition: Solubility reflects the free-energy balance of separating solute and solvent particles and forming new interactions, including entropy. Polarity and hydrogen bonding are useful guides, but molecular size, ionization, temperature, and crystal stability also matter.
major_error_concepts: Using like-dissolves-like as an exception-free quantitative law.
cards.prompt: What is Organic Solubility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dissolution depends on the overall free-energy balance, not polarity alone.

cards.definition: Boiling requires vapor pressure to match the external pressure. Intermolecular attractions, molecular size and shape, and pressure affect boiling points; a higher boiling point does not directly mean stronger covalent bonds within the molecule.
major_error_concepts: Equating higher boiling point automatically with stronger carbon-carbon bonds.
cards.prompt: What is Boiling Point and Structure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Boiling is a pressure-dependent phase equilibrium influenced by intermolecular interactions.

cards.definition: A Bronsted acid donates a proton and a Bronsted base accepts one, producing conjugate partners. Reaction direction depends on relative acid-base strengths in the relevant medium, not simply on which molecule visibly contains more hydrogen atoms.
major_error_concepts: Calling every hydrogen-containing molecule an equally strong proton donor.
cards.prompt: What is Organic Bronsted Acid and Base? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Proton transfer links conjugate acid-base pairs.

cards.definition: pKa is minus the base-ten logarithm of an acid dissociation constant under stated conditions. Lower pKa indicates a stronger acid in a comparable solvent and convention; values from different media are not automatically directly comparable.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a larger pKa means a stronger acid.
cards.prompt: What is pKa? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Lower pKa means stronger acidity within comparable conditions.

cards.definition: Stabilizing an acid's conjugate base generally favors deprotonation within a comparable setting. Charge-bearing atom, resonance, induction, hybridization, solvation, and aromaticity can all affect stability, so no single mnemonic ranks every pair correctly.
major_error_concepts: Ranking acids only by counting resonance drawings regardless of their validity or stability.
cards.prompt: What is Conjugate Base Stability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conjugate-base stability informs relative acidity under comparable conditions.

accepted_variants: Acid-base equilibrium from conjugate-acid pKa values.
cards.definition: For HA+B forming Aminus+BHplus, the equilibrium constant is approximately ten to the power pKa(BHplus)-pKa(HA) when the pKa values use a consistent medium and convention. Proton transfer favors the side with the weaker acid and weaker base.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the pKa difference so transfer is predicted toward the stronger acid.
cards.prompt: What is Proton Transfer Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Consistent pKa difference predicts proton-transfer equilibrium direction and scale.

accepted_variants: Bronsted basicity under a stated solvent.
cards.definition: Basicity measures the thermodynamic tendency to accept a proton under specified conditions. It differs from nucleophilicity, which describes reaction rate toward an electrophilic center; sterics, solvent, and the reaction partner can separate the two trends.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the strongest base is necessarily the fastest nucleophile for every substrate.
cards.prompt: What is Basicity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equilibrium proton affinity differs from kinetic attacking ability.

cards.definition: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a bond with an electrophilic center. It can be neutral or charged; electron availability, steric access, solvent, and the partner determine its reaction rate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming only negatively charged species can be nucleophiles.
cards.prompt: What is Nucleophile? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Electron-pair donor in bond formation.

cards.definition: An electrophile accepts an electron pair into a bond-forming interaction. Positive charge, polarized bonds, or accessible low-energy acceptor orbitals can confer electrophilicity, so the species need not carry an overall positive formal charge.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a neutral polarized carbonyl cannot be electrophilic.
cards.prompt: What is Electrophile? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Electron-pair acceptor in bond formation.

cards.definition: A curved arrow in a polar mechanism starts at an electron pair or bond and ends where that pair is assigned after the step. It tracks electron movement, not atom travel; electron counts and charges must remain consistent.
major_error_concepts: Starting an electron-pair arrow from an electron-deficient atom with no source electrons.
cards.prompt: What is Curved Arrow Mechanism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Arrow tail identifies electron source and head their destination.

cards.definition: Homolytic bond cleavage gives one bonding electron to each fragment, commonly producing radicals. Single-headed fishhook arrows represent one-electron movement, unlike the paired-electron arrows used for ordinary heterolytic steps.
major_error_concepts: Drawing both bonding electrons on one fragment while calling the step homolytic.
cards.prompt: What is Homolytic Cleavage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Bond electron pair splits one electron to each fragment.

cards.definition: Heterolytic bond cleavage assigns both bonding electrons to one fragment, often forming oppositely charged species. The favored direction depends on bonding, solvent, and stability, not on a universal rule that either fragment always retains electrons.
major_error_concepts: Assigning one electron to each fragment while labeling the process heterolytic.
cards.prompt: What is Heterolytic Cleavage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Both bonding electrons go to the same fragment.

accepted_variants: BDE or bond dissociation enthalpy with convention stated.
cards.definition: Bond dissociation energy characterizes the energy required for a specified homolytic bond cleavage, commonly in the gas phase. It helps compare radical bond-breaking energetics but is not identical to a reaction activation barrier or a solution-phase pKa.
major_error_concepts: Using a bond dissociation energy as the activation energy of every reaction involving that bond.
cards.prompt: What is Bond Dissociation Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Energy for specified homolytic bond cleavage.

cards.definition: Reaction thermodynamics compares the free energies of reactants and products and determines the equilibrium tendency under specified conditions. A favorable free-energy change does not imply a fast reaction because the path may contain a high activation barrier.
major_error_concepts: Equating a negative reaction free energy with immediate completion.
cards.prompt: What is Reaction Thermodynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Free-energy difference determines equilibrium, not rate by itself.

cards.definition: Chemical kinetics describes reaction rates and how they depend on concentrations, temperature, and mechanism. Rates depend on activation barriers and the operative pathway rather than only on the stability of final products.
major_error_concepts: Predicting the fastest product solely from which product is lowest in free energy.
cards.prompt: What is Reaction Kinetics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Rate and pathway dependence are distinct from equilibrium favorability.

cards.definition: A reaction-coordinate diagram plots a chosen energy measure along progress through a pathway. Maxima represent transition states and minima may represent reactants, intermediates, or products; the horizontal coordinate is not generally elapsed time.
major_error_concepts: Reading the width between peaks as the measured duration of a mechanistic step.
cards.prompt: What is Reaction Coordinate Diagram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Energy profile maps pathway barriers and minima, not an ordinary time trace.

cards.definition: An intermediate is a species corresponding to a local minimum on a reaction energy surface between elementary steps. It has a finite lifetime, though it may be too short-lived to isolate, and differs from a transition-state configuration at a barrier.
major_error_concepts: Calling every drawn transition state an isolable intermediate.
cards.prompt: What is Reaction Intermediate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Local energy minimum between mechanistic steps.

accepted_variants: Activated complex in the transition-state sense.
cards.definition: A transition state is a high-energy dividing configuration associated with crossing an elementary reaction barrier. It is not a stable species that accumulates in the same way as an intermediate, and its structure reflects partially changing bonds.
major_error_concepts: Placing a transition state at a stable energy minimum.
cards.prompt: What is Transition State? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Barrier-crossing configuration rather than a local-minimum species.

accepted_variants: Rate-limiting step under a justified approximation.
cards.definition: A rate-determining step is an approximate description of a step exerting dominant control on overall rate under specified conditions. Pre-equilibria and concentrations can make observed rate laws more complicated than simply copying the molecularity of the tallest-looking diagram peak.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the highest absolute peak always directly gives the observed rate law without considering preceding equilibria.
cards.prompt: What is Rate Determining Step? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dominant kinetic control is conditional on the full mechanism and concentrations.

cards.definition: A catalyst provides a pathway that changes reaction rate while being regenerated in the overall process. It does not change the equilibrium constant for the same overall reaction under the same conditions, although it can enable equilibrium to be approached faster.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a catalyst makes an unchanged equilibrium intrinsically favor products more strongly.
cards.prompt: What is Catalysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regenerated participant changes kinetics without changing the same reaction's equilibrium.

cards.definition: An alkane is a saturated acyclic hydrocarbon containing only carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen single bonds. Cycloalkanes share saturation but differ in ring connectivity and molecular-formula relationships.
major_error_concepts: Applying the acyclic formula CnH2n+2 to every cyclic saturated hydrocarbon.
cards.prompt: What is Alkane? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Saturated acyclic hydrocarbon with single bonds.

cards.definition: Systematic alkane naming identifies an appropriate parent chain, numbers it to locate substituents under the naming rules, and identifies those substituents consistently. The visually straightest drawn chain is not necessarily the required parent chain.
major_error_concepts: Choosing the parent solely from how straight a chain looks on paper.
cards.prompt: What is Alkane Nomenclature? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Parent selection, numbering, and substituent identification determine the name.

accepted_variants: Conformers or rotamers with restrictions acknowledged.
cards.definition: Conformations are spatial arrangements interconverted mainly by rotation about single bonds without changing connectivity. Different conformations can have different energies, and not every formally single bond rotates freely when conjugation or ring constraints matter.
major_error_concepts: Calling every bond rotation a change to a constitutional isomer.
cards.prompt: What is Conformation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Single-bond rotation changes conformation rather than constitution.

cards.definition: A Newman projection views a molecule along a selected bond, separating front- and back-atom substituent orientations. The viewing direction and atom assignment must be fixed before comparing staggered, eclipsed, anti, or gauche arrangements.
major_error_concepts: Comparing two projections without accounting for a reversed viewing direction.
cards.prompt: What is Newman Projection? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: End-on bond view distinguishes front and back substituents.

cards.definition: Torsional strain is an energy penalty associated with unfavorable eclipsing interactions during rotation about a bond. It differs conceptually from angle strain and can vary with the substituents and electronic structure.
major_error_concepts: Calling every unfavorable bond angle torsional strain.
cards.prompt: What is Torsional Strain? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Eclipsing-related rotational energy penalty.

accepted_variants: Steric hindrance or crowding when used in the appropriate context.
cards.definition: Steric strain arises when spatially crowded atoms or groups create unfavorable nonbonded interactions. Its size depends on the three-dimensional arrangement rather than only the number of substituents written in a formula.
major_error_concepts: Inferring steric effects solely from a two-dimensional drawing's spacing.
cards.prompt: What is Steric Strain? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Nonbonded crowding raises conformational or structural energy.

cards.definition: A cycloalkane contains a saturated carbon ring. Ring closure restricts conformations and can introduce angle, torsional, or other strain, so properties cannot be inferred by treating every bond as an independent acyclic rotation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming ring bonds rotate independently without affecting the rest of the ring.
cards.prompt: What is Cycloalkane? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Saturated ring connectivity constrains conformation.

accepted_variants: Angle, torsional, and transannular ring-strain contributions.
cards.definition: Ring strain combines energetic penalties from nonideal bond angles, torsional interactions, and sometimes nonbonded contacts across a ring. It depends on ring size and conformation rather than increasing uniformly with the number of ring atoms.
major_error_concepts: Assuming larger rings are always either more strained or less strained in one simple monotonic order.
cards.prompt: What is Ring Strain? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Several geometric and nonbonded contributions determine cyclic strain.

cards.definition: The chair conformation of cyclohexane has near-tetrahedral bond angles and largely staggered bonds, giving low strain. It is three-dimensional, with alternating bond orientations rather than a flat hexagon.
major_error_concepts: Treating a planar hexagon as the actual lowest-energy cyclohexane geometry.
cards.prompt: What is Cyclohexane Chair? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
