cards.prompt: What is Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It equates compactness with closedness and boundedness in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, turning an open-cover property into a practical test
the equivalence does not extend unchanged to arbitrary metric or infinite-dimensional spaces.
cards.term: Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space: role

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The characterization that a subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact exactly when closed and bounded.
major_error_concepts: Applying closed-and-bounded compactness to arbitrary metric spaces.
cards.prompt: State Heine-Borel theorem in Euclidean space, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The characterization that a subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact exactly when closed and bounded.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The pointwise condition that for every target tolerance there is a source radius which may depend on the point and tolerance.
major_error_concepts: Choosing delta dependent on the moving input point after quantification.
cards.prompt: Define Metric epsilon-delta continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The pointwise condition that for every target tolerance there is a source radius which may depend on the point and tolerance.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space theorem joining the two compactness formulations through total boundedness or a Lebesgue-number argument.
major_error_concepts: Claiming equivalence in arbitrary topological spaces.
cards.prompt: Define Open-cover and sequential compactness equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The metric-space theorem joining the two compactness formulations through total boundedness or a Lebesgue-number argument.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every open cover of a subset has a finite subcover with coverage relative to the ambient space declared.
major_error_concepts: Checking only one convenient cover.
cards.prompt: Define Open-cover compactness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that every open cover of a subset has a finite subcover with coverage relative to the ambient space declared.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every sequence in a subset has a subsequence converging to a point of that subset.
major_error_concepts: Allowing the subsequence limit outside the subset.
cards.prompt: Define Sequential compactness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that every sequence in a subset has a subsequence converging to a point of that subset.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space theorem that f is continuous at x exactly when x_n to x implies f(x_n) to f(x).
major_error_concepts: Checking only sequences chosen conveniently for f.
cards.prompt: Define Sequential continuity equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The metric-space theorem that f is continuous at x exactly when x_n to x implies f(x_n) to f(x).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that for every positive epsilon finitely many epsilon-balls cover the set which is stronger than boundedness in general.
major_error_concepts: Replacing epsilon-dependent finite nets with one bounded ball.
cards.prompt: Define Total boundedness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that for every positive epsilon finitely many epsilon-balls cover the set which is stronger than boundedness in general.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The global epsilon-delta condition with one delta for all domain points and the theorem that continuity on a compact metric domain implies it.
major_error_concepts: Confusing continuity at every point with a uniform choice on a noncompact set.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform continuity and Heine-Cantor. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The global epsilon-delta condition with one delta for all domain points and the theorem that continuity on a compact metric domain implies it.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The inequality definition and monotone-slope characterization of a convex function on an interval independent of differentiability.
major_error_concepts: Using a graph picture without the quantified inequality.
cards.prompt: Define Convexity by secant slopes. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The inequality definition and monotone-slope characterization of a convex function on an interval independent of differentiability.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a differentiable function is convex exactly when its derivative is nondecreasing with supporting-line consequences.
major_error_concepts: Assuming f'' exists when only f' monotonicity is needed.
cards.prompt: Define Convexity from derivative monotonicity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that a differentiable function is convex exactly when its derivative is nondecreasing with supporting-line consequences.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every derivative has the intermediate-value property even when the derivative is discontinuous.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every derivative is continuous.
cards.prompt: Define Darboux property of derivatives. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that every derivative has the intermediate-value property even when the derivative is discontinuous.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The sum product quotient and chain rules proved from difference quotients with all existence and nonzero conditions explicit.
major_error_concepts: Using the desired product rule inside its own proof.
cards.prompt: Define Derivative algebra rules from limits. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The sum product quotient and chain rules proved from difference quotients with all existence and nonzero conditions explicit.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The limit of the difference quotient at an accumulation point with domain-side and two-sided or one-sided convention explicit.
major_error_concepts: Reading a tangent from a graph as proof.
cards.prompt: Define Derivative as quantified linear rate. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The limit of the difference quotient at an accumulation point with domain-side and two-sided or one-sided convention explicit.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The mean-value argument that a nonnegative derivative on an interval implies nondecreasing behavior while an identically zero derivative implies constancy.
major_error_concepts: Inferring strictly increasing from a derivative that is merely nonnegative.
cards.prompt: Define Derivative-sign proof of interval monotonicity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The mean-value argument that a nonnegative derivative on an interval implies nondecreasing behavior while an identically zero derivative implies constancy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The quantified argument that a finite derivative at a point factors the function increment into a convergent hence bounded difference quotient and a vanishing input increment.
major_error_concepts: Assuming continuity implies differentiability or citing the implication without the factorization.
cards.prompt: Define Difference-quotient proof that differentiability forces continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: First material clause: The quantified argument that a finite derivative at a point factors the function increment
Remaining material clause: into a convergent hence bounded difference quotient and a vanishing input increment.
cards.term: Difference-quotient proof that differentiability forces continuity

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers differentiability through a locally invertible one-variable map and computes the inverse derivative as a reciprocal; the original derivative must be nonzero and local invertibility must be established.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula where f' vanishes or f is not one-to-one.
cards.prompt: What is Inverse derivative theorem in one variable used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It transfers differentiability through a locally invertible one-variable map and computes the inverse derivative as a reciprocal
the original derivative must be nonzero and local invertibility must be established.
cards.term: Inverse derivative theorem in one variable: role

cards.definition: Let f be continuous and strictly monotone on an open interval I, differentiable at a in I, with f'(a)≠0. Its inverse is differentiable at b=f(a), and (f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(a)=1/f'(f^{-1}(b)). Strict monotonicity and continuity ensure an interval image and a continuous inverse; this does not justify reciprocation where f'=0.
major_error_concepts: At every b, (f^{-1})'(b)=1/f'(b), regardless of whether b is the preimage point.
cards.prompt: State a one-variable inverse derivative theorem with sufficient interval hypotheses and the correct evaluation points.
required_concepts: Use an interval map with a continuous monotone inverse.
Require a nonzero derivative at the preimage a.
Evaluate the inverse derivative at f(a) and reciprocate f'(a).
cards.term: Inverse derivative theorem in one variable

cards.definition: **Definition.** The mean-value consequence that the absolute derivative is at most M on an interval and therefore the absolute output difference is at most M times the absolute input difference.
major_error_concepts: Using the result across disconnected domains.
cards.prompt: Define Lipschitz bound from bounded derivative. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The mean-value consequence that the absolute derivative is at most M on an interval
and therefore the absolute output difference is at most M times the absolute input difference.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Fermat's theorem that an interior differentiable local extremum has derivative zero with endpoint and nondifferentiable exceptions preserved.
major_error_concepts: Claiming derivative zero implies a local extremum.
cards.prompt: Define Local extremum derivative condition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Fermat's theorem that an interior differentiable local extremum has derivative zero with endpoint and nondifferentiable exceptions preserved.

cards.definition: **Proof idea.** Subtracting the endpoint secant line creates an auxiliary function with equal endpoint values. Rolle's theorem supplies an interior zero derivative for that function, which rearranges to the Mean Value Theorem conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Applying Rolle's theorem directly to the original function when its endpoint values differ, or omitting the continuity and differentiability hypotheses.
cards.prompt: Outline the auxiliary-function proof idea for the Mean Value Theorem.
required_concepts: Subtracting the endpoint secant line creates an auxiliary function with equal endpoint values.
Rolle's theorem supplies an interior zero derivative for the auxiliary function, which rearranges to the Mean Value Theorem conclusion.
cards.term: Auxiliary-function proof idea for the Mean Value Theorem

cards.definition: **Proof idea.** Continuity on the compact interval gives an attained extremum. If the equal-endpoint function is nonconstant, an attained maximum or minimum lies in the interior, where differentiability forces derivative zero; the constant case is immediate.
major_error_concepts: Claiming equal endpoint values alone place a maximum or minimum in the interior without separating the constant and nonconstant cases.
cards.prompt: Outline the extrema proof idea for Rolle's theorem.
required_concepts: Continuity on a compact interval gives an attained extremum.
If equal endpoint values do not make the function constant, one attained extremum is interior, where differentiability forces derivative zero; the constant case is immediate.
cards.term: Extrema proof idea for Rolle's theorem

cards.definition: **Definition.** The sufficient and under appropriate regularity equivalent condition f'' nonnegative for convexity.
major_error_concepts: Calling isolated positive second derivative global convexity.
cards.prompt: Define Second-derivative convexity criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The sufficient and under appropriate regularity equivalent condition f'' nonnegative for convexity.

accepted_variants: Let h(0)=0 and h(x)=x+exp(-1/x²) for x≠0. The flat exponential extends smoothly with all derivatives zero at 0, so h is C∞ and its Taylor series at 0 is x. Yet h(x)-x is positive for all nonzero x, so h is not analytic there. The Taylor coefficients need not all be zero.
cards.definition: Define f(0)=0 and f(x)=exp(-1/x²) for x≠0. This function is C∞ on R and every derivative at 0 is zero, so its Taylor series there is identically zero. Yet f(x)>0 for every x≠0, so that series fails to equal f on any neighborhood of 0. Thus smoothness does not imply analyticity.
major_error_concepts: The function |x| proves that C∞ functions can fail to be analytic at 0 because |x| is infinitely differentiable there.
cards.prompt: Give a smooth nonanalytic counterexample and explain exactly why its Taylor series fails to recover it.
required_concepts: Give an explicit function and justify smoothness on a neighborhood of the expansion point.
Identify its Taylor series and establish that the function differs from that series arbitrarily near the point.
Conclude C∞ does not imply analyticity; zero Taylor coefficients are only one possible construction.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The uniform consequence that a bound M on the next derivative yields absolute remainder at most M times the absolute displacement to the power n plus one divided by factorial n plus one.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a numerical approximation without a valid M.
cards.prompt: Define Taylor remainder error bound. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: First material clause: The uniform consequence that a bound M on the next derivative yields absolute remainder at most
Remaining material clause: M times the absolute displacement to the power n plus one divided by factorial n plus one.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It represents a smooth function by a local polynomial plus a derivative-controlled remainder, enabling approximation and error bounds; a formal Taylor series without remainder control need not equal the function.
major_error_concepts: Using a derivative bound not known on the interval between a and x.
cards.prompt: What is Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It represents a smooth function by a local polynomial plus a derivative-controlled remainder, enabling approximation and error bounds
a formal Taylor series without remainder control need not equal the function.
cards.term: Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder: role

cards.definition: If f is C^(n+1) on an interval containing a and x, then f(x)=sum_{k=0}^n f^(k)(a)(x-a)^k/k! + f^(n+1)(xi)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)! for some xi between a and x (the a=x case is immediate). The intermediate point may depend on x. The remainder term, not formal infinite-series notation alone, controls the approximation error.
major_error_concepts: Continuity of f alone guarantees every degree-n Taylor formula, with the same xi for all x.
cards.prompt: State Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder under a sufficient C^(n+1) interval hypothesis.
required_concepts: State a sufficient C^(n+1) interval hypothesis.
Give the Taylor polynomial plus the (n+1)st-derivative Lagrange remainder.
xi lies between the expansion and evaluation points and may depend on x.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It compares increments of two functions through their derivatives and underlies Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem and rigorous l'Hopital-style arguments; denominator derivative and nondegeneracy conditions cannot be ignored.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by the second derivative without proving it nonzero.
cards.prompt: What is Two-function cross-multiplied mean-value theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It compares increments of two functions through their derivatives and underlies Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem and rigorous l'Hopital-style arguments
denominator derivative and nondegeneracy conditions cannot be ignored.

cards.definition: If real functions f and g are continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with a<b, then some c in (a,b) satisfies [f(b)-f(a)]g'(c)=[g(b)-g(a)]f'(c). This cross-multiplied form requires no division and no nonzero derivative assumption. A quotient version additionally requires the relevant denominator quantities to be nonzero.
major_error_concepts: The cross-multiplied theorem guarantees [f(b)-f(a)]/[g(b)-g(a)]=f'(c)/g'(c) even when g is constant.
cards.prompt: State Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem in cross-multiplied form, and identify what is needed before dividing.
required_concepts: Both functions are continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on its interior.
State the cross-multiplied equality at one common interior c.
Nonzero denominator conditions are added only if dividing.

cards.definition: If f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] and |f(t)|≤M there, then F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt is M-Lipschitz: |F(y)-F(x)|≤M|y-x| for all x,y in [a,b]. Hence F is continuous even when f has discontinuities. Boundedness without Riemann integrability is not enough to define this F in the Riemann sense.
major_error_concepts: Every bounded function, including the rational-indicator Dirichlet function, defines a Riemann accumulation integral on a nondegenerate interval.
cards.prompt: Define Accumulation function continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: f is Riemann integrable on the interval.
A bound |f|≤M yields |F(y)-F(x)|≤M|y-x|.
Continuity of F does not assert differentiability at every point.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It shows that accumulating a continuous integrand creates an antiderivative and recovers the integrand by differentiation, linking local rates to area; weaker regularity changes the pointwise conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Replacing pointwise continuity with mere integrability or quoting antiderivative notation as proof.
cards.prompt: What is Accumulation-integral differentiation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It shows that accumulating a continuous integrand creates an antiderivative and recovers the integrand by differentiation, linking local rates to area
weaker regularity changes the pointwise conclusion.

cards.definition: Let f be Riemann integrable on [a,b] and continuous at c in (a,b). Then F(x)=integral_a^x f(t)dt is differentiable at c and F'(c)=f(c). Integrability makes F defined, while continuity at c establishes this pointwise derivative. Mere integrability alone does not guarantee the equality at every point.
major_error_concepts: Because f is Riemann integrable, F'(c)=f(c) must hold at every discontinuity as well.
cards.prompt: State the pointwise FTC for an accumulation integral, separating the integrability and continuity assumptions.
required_concepts: Require Riemann integrability on the interval.
Require continuity of f at the interior point c.
The accumulation derivative at c equals f(c).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that integrability and integral split at an interior point with partitions reconciled across both subintervals.
major_error_concepts: Double-counting or omitting the split point as a width contribution.
cards.prompt: Define Additivity over adjacent intervals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that integrability and integral split at an interior point with partitions reconciled across both subintervals.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The linearity monotonicity absolute-value and product integrability properties with boundedness and proof dependencies explicit.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion before proving the absolute-value function integrable.
cards.prompt: Define Algebra and order of integrals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The linearity monotonicity absolute-value and product integrability properties with boundedness and proof dependencies explicit.

cards.definition: If phi is C¹ on [a,b] and f is continuous on an interval containing phi([a,b]), then integral_a^b f(phi(t))phi'(t)dt = integral_{phi(a)}^{phi(b)} f(u)du. The derivative factor and oriented bounds are essential. In this continuous-integrand version phi need not be one-to-one or monotone; weaker Riemann-integrability variants require their own hypotheses.
major_error_concepts: Substitution removes phi'(t), and the new integral must always run from the smaller transformed endpoint to the larger one without a sign.
cards.prompt: State a continuous-integrand change-of-variables theorem for Riemann integrals, retaining orientation.
required_concepts: Use a C¹ change phi and continuous f on its image interval.
Transform both the differential factor and the oriented bounds.
Do not impose monotonicity as universally necessary for this version.
cards.term: Change of variables for Riemann integrals

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable via uniform continuity.
major_error_concepts: Using pointwise continuity with one undeclared global delta.
cards.prompt: Define Continuous-function integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that every continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable via uniform continuity.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It realizes the average value of a continuous integrand as an attained function value and supports weighted or physical mean interpretations; continuity and a nondegenerate interval matter, and the realizing point need not be unique.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion for an arbitrary integrable discontinuous function or confusing it with a derivative mean-value theorem.
cards.prompt: What is Continuous-integrand average-value theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It realizes the average value of a continuous integrand as an attained function value and supports weighted or physical mean interpretations
continuity and a nondegenerate interval matter, and the realizing point need not be unique.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The proof that a continuous real integrand on a compact interval attains the value of its integral divided by interval length using extremum bounds and connected image.
major_error_concepts: Using the conclusion for an arbitrary integrable discontinuous function or confusing it with a derivative mean-value theorem.
cards.prompt: State Continuous-integrand average-value theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The proof that a continuous real integrand on a compact interval attains the value of its integral divided by interval length using extremum bounds
and connected image.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The equality of upper and lower integrals equivalently for every epsilon a partition with upper-minus-lower sum below epsilon.
major_error_concepts: Checking one small numerical gap for a fixed epsilon.
cards.prompt: Define Darboux integrability criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The equality of upper and lower integrals equivalently for every epsilon a partition with upper-minus-lower sum below epsilon.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The everywhere-discontinuous rational-indicator function whose every subinterval has infimum zero and supremum one.
major_error_concepts: Choosing sample points to make a favorable Riemann sum.
cards.prompt: Define Dirichlet nonintegrability example. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The everywhere-discontinuous rational-indicator function whose every subinterval has infimum zero and supremum one.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite ordered subdivision of one compact interval with subinterval convention and maximum subinterval length declared for Darboux and Riemann arguments.
major_error_concepts: Treating an infinite grid or unordered sample as a Riemann partition.
cards.prompt: Define Finite Riemann partition and mesh. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A finite ordered subdivision of one compact interval with subinterval convention and maximum subinterval length declared for Darboux and Riemann arguments.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The definition of an unbounded-interval or singular-endpoint integral as a limit of proper integrals with convergence proved separately.
major_error_concepts: Treating the infinity symbol as an endpoint in a Riemann partition.
cards.prompt: Define Improper-integral boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The definition of an unbounded-interval or singular-endpoint integral as a limit of proper integrals with convergence proved separately.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers a derivative between factors in an integral and is the integral counterpart of the product rule, supporting estimates and transform identities; boundary terms and regularity assumptions must be retained.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula when required derivatives are not integrable.
cards.prompt: What is Integration by parts theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It transfers a derivative between factors in an integral and is the integral counterpart of the product rule, supporting estimates and transform identities
boundary terms and regularity assumptions must be retained.

cards.definition: If u,v are C¹ on [a,b], then integral_a^b u(t)v'(t)dt = u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-integral_a^b u'(t)v(t)dt. Both integrals exist under these hypotheses. More general valid versions are acceptable if their regularity and integrability assumptions are stated.
major_error_concepts: Integration by parts gives integral u v'=uv+integral u'v with no boundary evaluation.
cards.prompt: State definite integration by parts under sufficient regularity hypotheses.
required_concepts: State the boundary product evaluated at b minus a.
The remaining integral has a minus sign and moves the derivative from v to u.
Give C¹ functions as a sufficient hypothesis or a correct qualified weaker version.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that every bounded monotone function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable by telescoping oscillation control.
major_error_concepts: Assuming monotone functions are continuous.
cards.prompt: Define Monotone-function integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that every bounded monotone function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable by telescoping oscillation control.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The characterization that a bounded function is integrable when high-oscillation sets can be covered with sufficiently small total interval length at first-course depth.
major_error_concepts: Invoking measure-zero language without constructing the required covers.
cards.prompt: Define Oscillation criterion for Riemann integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: First material clause: The characterization that a bounded function is integrable when high-oscillation sets
Remaining material clause: can be covered with sufficiently small total interval length at first-course depth.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It evaluates a definite integral from any antiderivative and completes the bridge between differentiation and integration; existence of an antiderivative under the theorem's hypotheses must not be assumed for arbitrary functions.
major_error_concepts: Using an arbitrary antiderivative when its derivative is not known Riemann integrable.
cards.prompt: What is Riemann antiderivative evaluation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It evaluates a definite integral from any antiderivative and completes the bridge between differentiation and integration
existence of an antiderivative under the theorem's hypotheses must not be assumed for arbitrary functions.

cards.definition: Suppose F is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and its derivative has a Riemann-integrable extension f to [a,b]. Then integral_a^b f(x)dx=F(b)-F(a). Endpoint values assigned to f do not affect the integral. An arbitrary derivative need not be Riemann integrable, so the integrability premise is substantive.
major_error_concepts: Every derivative is automatically Riemann integrable, so an antiderivative symbol alone proves the evaluation formula.
cards.prompt: State the Riemann antiderivative evaluation theorem, including the derivative-integrability requirement.
required_concepts: F is continuous through the endpoints and differentiable in the interior.
Its derivative is Riemann integrable after harmless endpoint assignment.
The integral equals F(b)-F(a).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The integrability of functions with finitely many jumps or finitely many continuous pieces after isolating discontinuities.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every function with infinitely many discontinuities is nonintegrable.
cards.prompt: Define Step and piecewise-continuous integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The integrability of functions with finitely many jumps or finitely many continuous pieces after isolating discontinuities.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The infimum of upper sums and supremum of lower sums with lower integral never exceeding upper integral.
major_error_concepts: Taking the infimum and supremum in the wrong directions.
cards.prompt: Define Upper and lower Darboux integrals. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The infimum of upper sums and supremum of lower sums with lower integral never exceeding upper integral.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The sums of subinterval suprema or infima times widths for a bounded function with their order under refinement.
major_error_concepts: Assuming upper and lower sums use sampled values.
cards.prompt: Define Upper and lower Darboux sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The sums of subinterval suprema or infima times widths for a bounded function with their order under refinement.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns uniform boundedness or pointwise precompactness plus equicontinuity into a uniformly convergent subsequence, providing compactness for families of functions; pointwise boundedness without equicontinuity is insufficient.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform boundedness alone gives compactness.
cards.prompt: What is Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It turns uniform boundedness or pointwise precompactness plus equicontinuity into a uniformly convergent subsequence, providing compactness for families of functions
pointwise boundedness without equicontinuity is insufficient.
cards.term: Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth: role

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The compactness criterion that an equicontinuous pointwise relatively compact or uniformly bounded real-valued family on a compact metric domain has uniformly convergent subsequences.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform boundedness alone gives compactness.
cards.prompt: State Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: First material clause: The compactness criterion that an equicontinuous pointwise relatively compact or uniformly
Remaining material clause: bounded real-valued family on a compact metric domain has uniformly convergent subsequences.
cards.term: Arzela-Ascoli theorem at metric honors depth

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that bounded functions into a complete scalar field form a complete normed space under the supremum norm.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every function subspace is closed and complete.
cards.prompt: Define Completeness of bounded-function sup norm. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that bounded functions into a complete scalar field form a complete normed space under the supremum norm.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It supplies conditions under which a limit of differentiable functions remains differentiable with derivative equal to the derivative limit; pointwise convergence of functions and derivatives alone is generally too weak.
major_error_concepts: Assuming uniform convergence of f_n alone preserves derivatives.
cards.prompt: What is Derivative-limit interchange theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It supplies conditions under which a limit of differentiable functions remains differentiable with derivative equal to the derivative limit
pointwise convergence of functions and derivatives alone is generally too weak.

cards.definition: A sufficient version is: f_n are C¹ on a fixed compact interval [a,b], f_n(x_0) converges at some x_0 in [a,b], and f_n' converges uniformly there to g. Then f_n converges uniformly to a C¹ function f and f'=g on the interval interior, with one-sided endpoint derivatives. On a disconnected domain, one anchor point does not control arbitrary constants on other components.
major_error_concepts: Uniform convergence of derivatives on two disjoint intervals plus one anchor on the first controls additive constants on the second.
cards.prompt: State a sufficient compact-interval theorem for interchanging differentiation and a sequence limit.
required_concepts: Use a fixed compact interval and C¹ functions as sufficient regularity.
Derivative convergence is uniform and function values converge at one anchor.
The functions converge uniformly to a differentiable limit whose derivative is g.

accepted_variants: Another example is f_n(x)=sin(n²x)/n on R. The bound |f_n|≤1/n proves uniform convergence to 0, but f_n'(0)=n diverges rather than approaching the derivative 0 of the limit.
cards.definition: Take f_n(x)=sin(nx)/n on R. Since |f_n(x)|≤1/n for every x, f_n→0 uniformly. But f_n'(x)=cos(nx), and at x=pi these derivatives alternate between -1 and 1 rather than converge to the derivative 0 of the limit. Thus even uniform function convergence does not by itself justify derivative convergence.
major_error_concepts: The uniform bound on sin(nx)/n forces cos(nx) to converge to zero at every x.
cards.prompt: Give a uniformly convergent sequence of differentiable functions for which derivative convergence fails, and verify the failure.
required_concepts: Give an explicit sequence of differentiable functions.
Verify uniform convergence of the functions to their stated limit.
Show at a specified point that their derivatives do not converge to the derivative of the limit; the reference sine sequence is only one valid witness.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It upgrades monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to uniform convergence on a compact space when the limit is continuous; each compactness, monotonicity, and continuity condition carries real force.
major_error_concepts: Dropping compactness continuity or monotonicity.
cards.prompt: What is Dini theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It upgrades monotone pointwise convergence of continuous functions to uniform convergence on a compact space when the limit is continuous
each compactness, monotonicity, and continuity condition carries real force.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The compact-domain result that monotone pointwise convergence of continuous real functions to a continuous limit is uniform.
major_error_concepts: Dropping compactness continuity or monotonicity.
cards.prompt: State Dini theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The compact-domain result that monotone pointwise convergence of continuous real functions to a continuous limit is uniform.

accepted_variants: On [0,1], f_n(x)=min(1,nx) is continuous and converges pointwise to f(0)=0 and f(x)=1 for x>0. The limit is discontinuous at 0, so convergence cannot be uniform. This is a different valid witness from x^n.
cards.definition: On [0,1], let f_n(x)=x^n. Each f_n is continuous. The pointwise limit is 0 for 0≤x<1 and 1 at x=1, so it is discontinuous at 1. The convergence is not uniform: the supremum error remains 1, although it is approached rather than attained on x<1. This does not contradict preservation of continuity by uniform limits.
major_error_concepts: x^n converges uniformly on [0,1] to a discontinuous function, disproving continuity preservation by uniform convergence.
cards.prompt: What claim does Discontinuous pointwise-limit counterexample refute, and why?
required_concepts: Give continuous functions on a common domain and identify their pointwise limit.
Exhibit and justify a discontinuity of that limit.
Explain why this does not contradict continuity preservation under uniform convergence; the x^n witness is illustrative, not mandatory.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The common local modulus property controlling all family members at once with uniform equicontinuity distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Confusing bounded function values with equicontinuity.
cards.prompt: Define Equicontinuity of a function family. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The common local modulus property controlling all family members at once with uniform equicontinuity distinguished.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The explicit mapping from each desired continuity integral derivative sum or power-series interchange to its sufficient hypotheses counterexamples and proof dependency.
major_error_concepts: Using interchange by visual symmetry of notation.
cards.prompt: Define Limit-operation dependency matrix. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: First material clause: The explicit mapping from each desired continuity integral derivative sum or power-series
Remaining material clause: interchange to its sufficient hypotheses counterexamples and proof dependency.

cards.definition: A sequence f_n converges pointwise to f on X if for every x in X and epsilon>0 there is N=N(x,epsilon) such that n≥N implies |f_n(x)-f(x)|<epsilon. Dependence on x is permitted, not required. A single N working for all x proves the stronger property of uniform convergence and is also a valid proof of pointwise convergence.
major_error_concepts: To show pointwise convergence, for each n one may choose a convenient x_n and check only f_n(x_n).
cards.prompt: Define pointwise convergence, and explain whether a uniform convergence proof also establishes it.
required_concepts: For each fixed x and epsilon, one index controls all later n.
N may depend on x.
A uniform bound is stronger but must still be accepted as proving pointwise convergence.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It makes polynomials uniformly dense in continuous functions on a compact interval, justifying approximation by algebraic models; it is an existence theorem and does not supply the best degree, coefficients, or approximation rate by itself.
major_error_concepts: Calling one Taylor polynomial a uniform approximation theorem for every continuous function.
cards.prompt: What is Polynomial approximation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It makes polynomials uniformly dense in continuous functions on a compact interval, justifying approximation by algebraic models
it is an existence theorem and does not supply the best degree, coefficients, or approximation rate by itself.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The Weierstrass conclusion that continuous real functions on a compact interval can be uniformly approximated by polynomials with proof route and scope explicit.
major_error_concepts: Calling one Taylor polynomial a uniform approximation theorem for every continuous function.
cards.prompt: State Polynomial approximation theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The Weierstrass conclusion that continuous real functions on a compact interval can be uniformly approximated by polynomials with proof route
and scope explicit.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that inside the radius of convergence a power series is continuous and may be integrated and differentiated termwise with the derived series sharing the radius.
major_error_concepts: Including endpoints without separate convergence checks.
cards.prompt: Define Power-series termwise operations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that inside the radius of convergence a power series is continuous
and may be integrated and differentiated termwise with the derived series sharing the radius.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The supremum over the domain of the absolute function value whose induced metric makes uniform convergence exactly norm convergence.
major_error_concepts: Using the maximum when the supremum is not attained.
cards.prompt: Define Supremum norm on bounded functions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The supremum over the domain of the absolute function value whose induced metric makes uniform convergence exactly norm convergence.

cards.definition: If each f_n is Riemann integrable on a fixed finite interval [a,b] and f_n→f uniformly there, then f is Riemann integrable and integral_a^b f_n→integral_a^b f. Indeed the integral error is at most (b-a) sup_{x in [a,b]}|f_n(x)-f(x)|. The finite-domain factor is essential; uniform convergence on an unbounded interval needs additional tail control.
major_error_concepts: Uniform convergence on [0,infinity) always permits exchanging the limit and improper integral without tail assumptions.
cards.prompt: Define Termwise Riemann integration under uniform convergence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Use one fixed finite interval and Riemann-integrable f_n.
Require uniform convergence.
The limit is integrable and the integral error is bounded by interval length times sup error.
cards.term: Termwise Riemann integration under uniform convergence

cards.definition: **Definition.** The criterion that for every epsilon all sufficiently late functions are uniformly close at every domain point with completeness of codomain needed for the converse.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a limit exists in an incomplete codomain.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform Cauchy criterion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: First material clause: The criterion that for every epsilon all sufficiently late functions are uniformly
Remaining material clause: close at every domain point with completeness of codomain needed for the converse.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The convergence of its partial-sum functions uniformly with absolute uniform convergence distinguished from conditional uniform behavior.
major_error_concepts: Calling pointwise absolute convergence uniform absolute convergence.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform convergence of a function series. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The convergence of its partial-sum functions uniformly with absolute uniform convergence distinguished from conditional uniform behavior.
cards.term: Uniform convergence of a function series

cards.definition: **Definition.** The quantifier order where for every epsilon one N works for all domain points equivalently the sup error tends to zero when finite.
major_error_concepts: Checking finitely many x values.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform convergence of functions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The quantifier order where for every epsilon one N works for all domain points equivalently the sup error tends to zero when finite.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous proved by a three-term epsilon estimate.
major_error_concepts: Replacing uniform convergence with pointwise convergence.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform limit of continuous functions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous proved by a three-term epsilon estimate.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that uniform absolute bounds on each f_n by M_n with sum M_n convergent imply uniform absolute convergence of the function series.
major_error_concepts: Choosing M_n depending on x.
cards.prompt: Define Weierstrass M-test. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that uniform absolute bounds on each f_n by M_n with sum M_n convergent imply uniform absolute convergence of the function series.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The epsilon-delta control of sums of function increments over disjoint intervals and its stronger relation to the fundamental theorem than uniform continuity.
major_error_concepts: Equating absolute continuity with uniform continuity.
cards.prompt: Define Absolute continuity preview. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The epsilon-delta control of sums of function increments over disjoint intervals and its stronger relation to the fundamental theorem than uniform continuity.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The complete-metric-space theorem that a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense and its distinction from measure size.
major_error_concepts: Calling meagre equivalent to measure zero.
cards.prompt: Define Baire-category preview. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The complete-metric-space theorem that a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense and its distinction from measure size.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns a contraction on a complete metric space into a unique fixed point and a convergent iteration with quantitative error control, supporting existence and algorithms simultaneously; a merely continuous or noncontractive map does not receive the guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Dropping completeness or the self-map condition.
cards.prompt: What is Banach fixed-point theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It turns a contraction on a complete metric space into a unique fixed point and a convergent iteration with quantitative error control, supporting existence and algorithms simultaneously
a merely continuous or noncontractive map does not receive the guarantee.

cards.definition: Let T:X→X be a contraction with one factor 0≤q<1 on a nonempty complete metric space. Then T has a unique fixed point x*, and for every x_0 in X, x_(n+1)=T(x_n) converges to x*. In particular d(x_n,x*)≤q^n d(x_0,x*) for n≥1. Completeness, the self-map condition, and a uniform factor cannot simply be omitted.
major_error_concepts: On X=(0,1), T(x)=x/2 has a fixed point in X because it is a contraction, despite X not being complete.
cards.prompt: State the Banach fixed-point theorem with its space, self-map, uniform-factor, and convergence hypotheses.
required_concepts: The metric space is nonempty and complete.
T is a self-map with one contraction factor q<1.
There is a unique fixed point and every starting point converges geometrically.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The continuous nondecreasing function constant on removed intervals whose derivative is zero where defined off the Cantor set yet whose total rise is one.
major_error_concepts: Concluding zero derivative almost everywhere implies constant without the right hypotheses and measure theory.
cards.prompt: Define Cantor-function pathology. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The continuous nondecreasing function constant on removed intervals whose derivative is zero where defined off the Cantor set yet whose total rise is one.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nested closed-set construction deleting middle thirds with compactness uncountability empty interior and zero-length-cover properties separated.
major_error_concepts: Calling it countable because it has no intervals.
cards.prompt: Define Cantor-set construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nested closed-set construction deleting middle thirds with compactness uncountability empty interior and zero-length-cover properties separated.

cards.definition: A contraction on a metric space (X,d) is a self-map T:X→X for which one constant q with 0≤q<1 satisfies d(Tx,Ty)≤q d(x,y) for every x,y in X. A separate factor for each pair, or merely strict shortening without a uniform q<1, is not the Banach-contraction hypothesis.
major_error_concepts: Any self-map that brings each distinct pair strictly closer is a Banach contraction, even when no common q<1 works.
cards.prompt: Define a Banach contraction and distinguish a uniform contraction factor from merely pairwise strict shortening.
required_concepts: T maps the space into itself.
One common q in [0,1) works for every pair.
Point-dependent shortening factors need not give a contraction.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The controlled reformulation of an initial-value problem as an integral fixed-point equation on a complete function space under a local contraction bound.
major_error_concepts: Calling the illustrative proof a full ODE existence theory.
cards.prompt: Define Fixed-point formulation of an initial-value problem. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The controlled reformulation of an initial-value problem as an integral fixed-point equation on a complete function space under a local contraction bound.
cards.term: Fixed-point formulation of an initial-value problem

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that a real bounded-variation function is a difference of two increasing functions with normalization and uniqueness qualifications.
major_error_concepts: Confusing this with Jordan canonical form or measure decomposition.
cards.prompt: Define Jordan decomposition for bounded variation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem that a real bounded-variation function is a difference of two increasing functions with normalization and uniqueness qualifications.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A continuous function lacking a finite derivative at every point and demonstrating that continuity gives no generic smoothness.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a jagged plot is proof of nowhere differentiability.
cards.prompt: Define Nowhere-differentiable continuous function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A continuous function lacking a finite derivative at every point and demonstrating that continuity gives no generic smoothness.

cards.definition: Under the Banach fixed-point hypotheses, set x_(n+1)=T(x_n) and let 0≤q<1 be a verified global contraction factor. For n≥1, d(x_n,x*)≤q^n d(x_1,x_0)/(1-q) is an a priori bound, while d(x_n,x*)≤q d(x_n,x_(n-1))/(1-q) is an a posteriori bound. A factor estimated from a few observed iterate ratios is not automatically a valid global q.
major_error_concepts: The distance to the fixed point is always at most the latest step size, independently of q.
cards.prompt: State the a priori and a posteriori error bounds for Picard iteration under a verified contraction factor.
required_concepts: State the indexed a priori bound q^n d(x_1,x_0)/(1-q).
State the a posteriori bound q d(x_n,x_(n-1))/(1-q).
The contraction factor is a proved uniform bound, not just an observed ratio.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The narrow statement supported by exact hypotheses proofs counterexamples and reviews with numerical empirical learner and downstream claims denied.
major_error_concepts: Calling course artifact completion proof of research-level analysis mastery.
cards.prompt: Define Qualified Real Analysis I conclusion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The narrow statement supported by exact hypotheses proofs counterexamples and reviews with numerical empirical learner and downstream claims denied.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The explicit comparison of pointwise versus uniform Cauchy versus convergent local versus global and for-every/there-exists arrangements.
major_error_concepts: Swapping words without reversing all quantifiers.
cards.prompt: Define quantifier-order distinction.
required_concepts: The explicit comparison of pointwise versus uniform Cauchy versus convergent local versus global and for-every/there-exists arrangements.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The limit or Darboux-style integral of f against increments of a monotone or bounded-variation integrator alpha with both roles distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Replacing d alpha with alpha'(x)dx when the derivative does not represent all variation.
cards.prompt: Define Riemann-Stieltjes integral. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The limit or Darboux-style integral of f against increments of a monotone or bounded-variation integrator alpha with both roles distinguished.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity integral f d alpha plus integral alpha d f equals endpoint product difference under conditions guaranteeing both integrals.
major_error_concepts: Using the identity before proving both Stieltjes integrals exist.
cards.prompt: Define Stieltjes integration by parts. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The identity integral f d alpha plus integral alpha d f equals endpoint product difference under conditions guaranteeing both integrals.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The supremum over partitions of sums of absolute increments with bounded variation meaning finite total variation.
major_error_concepts: Using one partition sum as the total variation.
cards.prompt: Define Total variation of a function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The supremum over partitions of sums of absolute increments with bounded variation meaning finite total variation.

catalog.description: Develop rigorous arguments about the real numbers, sequences, series, continuity, differentiation, compactness, uniform convergence, and Riemann integration.
catalog.subject: Mathematics
catalog.title: Real Analysis I

cards.definition: A target population is the set of units about which a study intends to draw conclusions, defined by explicit membership and time boundaries. It can differ from the units actually reachable through the sampling frame.
major_error_concepts: Defining the population only as the people who happened to respond.
cards.prompt: What is Target Population? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Explicit set of intended inference units.
Membership and reference time are specified.

cards.definition: A finite population contains a fixed finite number N of units for the reference period. In design-based inference, their values are treated as fixed and randomness comes from how the sample is selected.
major_error_concepts: Assuming design-based analysis requires the population itself to be an IID random sample.
cards.prompt: What is Finite Population? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Finite set of N units.
Selection supplies design-based randomness.

cards.definition: A sample is the subset or selected collection of population units observed under a sampling procedure. Its realized composition differs from the sampling design, which specifies how possible samples could be selected.
major_error_concepts: Equating one realized sample with the full sampling design.
cards.prompt: What is Sample? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Selected units, distinct from the selection rule.

cards.definition: A sampling unit is an entity eligible for selection at a specified stage, such as a school or household. It need not be the final entity whose outcome is analyzed.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the sampling unit must always equal the analysis unit.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Selectable entity at a stated sampling stage.

accepted_variants: Unit of observation versus unit of analysis.
cards.definition: An observation unit is the entity on which a measurement is recorded; an analysis unit is the entity represented by the inferential target. A respondent may report measurements for other observation units, so these roles should be distinguished.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the person answering a household survey is necessarily the unit for every recorded variable.
cards.prompt: What is Observation and Analysis Units? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Measurement, analysis, and respondent roles can differ.

cards.definition: A sampling frame is the operational list or selection mechanism from which candidate units can be sampled. Its coverage of the target population must account for excluded, duplicated, outdated, or ineligible entries.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every available contact list perfectly covers the target population.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Operational basis for sample selection.
Frame coverage is not automatic.

cards.definition: Coverage error arises when the frame and target population do not align, including missing eligible units or including ineligible ones. It is distinct from eligible sampled units failing to respond.
major_error_concepts: Calling frame omissions ordinary sampling variation that necessarily vanishes with a larger sample.
cards.prompt: What is Coverage Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mismatch between frame coverage and target population.
Distinct from nonresponse.

accepted_variants: Quantity of scientific or descriptive interest.
cards.definition: An estimand is the precisely defined population quantity a study aims to estimate. It specifies the variable, population, reference period, and summary, rather than merely naming a statistical procedure.
major_error_concepts: Calling a software command the estimand without naming the target quantity.
cards.prompt: What is Survey Estimand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Target quantity with population and variable definition.

cards.definition: A finite-population total is T=sum over all N units of y_i. It counts the aggregate quantity in the specified population and differs from a total calculated only over the sample.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an unweighted sample total as the population total without a valid expansion.
cards.prompt: What is Population Total? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sum over every population unit.

cards.definition: A finite-population mean is the population total divided by N. Its target is an average per population unit, so an estimate of a total must be normalized appropriately to estimate the mean.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by the realized sample size when converting the actual population total to a population mean.
cards.prompt: What is Population Mean? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Population sum divided by population size.

accepted_variants: Population fraction or prevalence of a defined attribute.
cards.definition: A population proportion is the mean of a zero-one indicator for a defined characteristic. Its numerator counts eligible units with that characteristic and its denominator counts all units in the target population or stated domain.
major_error_concepts: Changing the denominator without changing the reported estimand.
cards.prompt: What is Population Proportion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mean of a binary indicator.
Denominator matches the target population.

cards.definition: A census seeks observations from every unit in the target population. It removes sample-selection variation only when enumeration is complete, but coverage, nonresponse, measurement, and processing errors can still occur.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any census necessarily measures the population without error.
cards.prompt: What is Census? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Attempted complete enumeration.
Nonsampling errors remain possible.

cards.definition: A sampling design is a probability rule assigning chances to possible samples. It specifies stages, replacement, selection probabilities, and constraints needed to understand an estimator's sampling behavior.
major_error_concepts: Treating an undocumented realized sample as a fully specified probability design.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Design? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability distribution over possible samples.

cards.definition: Probability sampling selects units through a known random mechanism with positive inclusion probabilities for the target units. It supports design-based inference when the design and response issues are handled appropriately.
major_error_concepts: Calling a voluntary opt-in sample a probability sample solely because it is large.
cards.prompt: What is Probability Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Known random selection and positive inclusion probabilities.

cards.definition: A nonprobability sample does not give every target unit a known selection probability through a documented random design. Generalization then relies on additional modeling, selection assumptions, or external information rather than design randomization alone.
major_error_concepts: Claiming demographic resemblance alone supplies known inclusion probabilities.
cards.prompt: What is Nonprobability Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unknown or nonrandom selection probabilities.
Population inference needs additional assumptions.

cards.definition: Simple random sampling without replacement selects n distinct units so every subset of size n has equal probability. Each unit has inclusion probability n/N, but selections are not independent because the sample size is fixed.
major_error_concepts: Assuming independent selection indicators in fixed-size sampling without replacement.
cards.prompt: What is Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equal probability for all n-unit subsets.
Distinct selections with inclusion probability n/N.

cards.definition: Simple random sampling with replacement takes independent uniform draws from the population, allowing repeats. Draw probability is 1/N, while a unit's probability of appearing at least once across n draws is generally not n/N.
major_error_concepts: Confusing per-draw probability with the probability of ever being selected.
cards.prompt: What is Simple Random Sampling With Replacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent equal-probability draws, repeats allowed.
Draw probability differs from eventual inclusion probability.

cards.definition: The first-order inclusion probability pi_i is the probability that unit i belongs to the final sample. It is a design probability, not the unit's realized zero-one membership or necessarily its per-draw selection chance.
major_error_concepts: Substituting a draw probability for inclusion probability in a design where they differ.
cards.prompt: What is Inclusion Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability of final sample inclusion.

cards.definition: The second-order inclusion probability pi_ij is the probability that both units i and j are included. Joint inclusion probabilities determine selection dependence and enter design-based variance formulas.
major_error_concepts: Assuming pi_ij always equals pi_i times pi_j under without-replacement sampling.
cards.prompt: What is Joint Inclusion Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability of joint inclusion.
Encodes dependence between selections.

accepted_variants: Design weight or inverse-probability sampling weight.
cards.definition: A base sampling weight is 1/pi_i for a unit with positive inclusion probability. It expands the selected unit according to its representation under the design, before separate nonresponse or calibration adjustments.
major_error_concepts: Using inclusion probability itself as the expansion weight.
cards.prompt: What is Base Sampling Weight? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Inverse inclusion probability.
Base weight precedes later adjustments.

cards.definition: A sample inclusion indicator I_i equals one if unit i is selected and zero otherwise. Its design expectation is pi_i, allowing sampled estimators to be written as sums across the fixed population.
major_error_concepts: Treating I_i as a continuously varying selection probability.
cards.prompt: What is Inclusion Indicator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Binary selection indicator with expectation pi_i.

cards.definition: Design expectation averages over possible samples drawn from the stated design while holding finite-population values fixed. It differs from expectation over a model that randomly generates the population values.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the actual sampling design with an IID population model without stating the change.
cards.prompt: What is Design Expectation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Average over random sample selection.
Population values held fixed.

cards.definition: An estimator is design-unbiased when its expectation over the sampling design equals the finite-population estimand. This does not mean every realized estimate is correct or that nonresponse cannot introduce bias.
major_error_concepts: Claiming unbiasedness means zero error in each sample.
cards.prompt: What is Design Unbiasedness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Design expectation equals target.

cards.definition: Sampling variance is the variance of an estimator across samples generated by the design. It measures random selection variability around the design expectation, not all sources of survey error.
major_error_concepts: Calling sampling variance a complete measure of coverage and measurement bias.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeated-design variability of the estimator.

cards.definition: A standard error is the square root of an estimator's variance, usually estimated from the sample and design information. It is measured in the estimator's units, unlike the variance.
major_error_concepts: Confusing standard error of a mean with standard deviation of individual outcomes.
cards.prompt: What is Standard Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Square root of estimator variance.

cards.definition: Sampling bias is systematic distortion arising when selection or frame coverage does not support the intended population inference. Increasing the size of a systematically selective convenience sample does not by itself eliminate that bias.
major_error_concepts: Treating a very large convenience sample as automatically representative.
cards.prompt: What is Sampling Bias? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Systematic selection-related distortion.
Larger samples do not automatically remove selection bias.

cards.definition: Mean squared error is expected squared deviation of an estimator from its target. When finite, it equals variance plus squared bias, so low variance alone does not guarantee accurate estimation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a highly precise but badly biased estimator necessarily accurate.
cards.prompt: What is Mean Squared Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: MSE equals variance plus bias squared.

cards.definition: Design consistency means an estimator approaches the target in probability along a specified sequence of growing populations and sampling designs. It is an asymptotic property and does not imply exact unbiasedness in a finite sample.
major_error_concepts: Equating consistency with exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
cards.prompt: What is Design Consistency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Convergence under a stated design asymptotic sequence.

cards.definition: The finite-population correction reflects reduced variance when sampling without replacement takes a substantial fraction f=n/N of a finite population. In the usual SRS mean variance formula it contributes the factor 1-f.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same correction automatically to independent with-replacement draws.
cards.prompt: What is Finite-Population Correction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Without-replacement variance reduction depends on sample fraction.

cards.definition: Under SRS without replacement, Var(ybar)=(1-n/N)S squared/n, where S squared uses denominator N-1 in the population. Replacing S squared by the sample variance gives the usual unbiased variance estimate when n exceeds one.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the sample fraction when it is large while claiming the exact finite-population formula.
cards.prompt: What is SRS Mean Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct SRS mean variance with FPC.
Variance convention is specified.

cards.definition: Under fixed-size SRS, the expansion estimator for a total is N times the sample mean. Its variance is N squared times the sample-mean variance when N is known.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying the mean variance by N rather than N squared.
cards.prompt: What is SRS Total Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Estimated total N times sample mean.
Variance scales by N squared.

cards.definition: A sample proportion under SRS is the sample mean of a binary indicator. Its uncertainty follows the corresponding mean-variance calculation, with finite-population and small-count issues considered as appropriate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a proportion estimate has zero uncertainty because each observation is only zero or one.
cards.prompt: What is SRS Proportion Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Indicator mean with design-aware variance.

cards.definition: A design-based confidence interval uses an estimator and a design-appropriate uncertainty method to achieve repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions. The fixed finite-population parameter is not repeatedly randomized by the interval procedure.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a realized frequentist interval assigns a posterior probability to the fixed parameter without a Bayesian model.
cards.prompt: What is Design-Based Confidence Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeated-design coverage for a fixed target.
Appropriate uncertainty method required.

cards.definition: A margin of error is the half-width of a stated interval, often a critical value times a standard error. It depends on coverage level, design, and estimator, and usually excludes nonsampling biases.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a margin of error as a bound on every possible survey bias.
cards.prompt: What is Margin of Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Interval half-width under specified assumptions.
Not total survey error.

cards.definition: Precision-based sample-size planning chooses n to reach a target interval width or estimation error under stated variability, design, and coverage assumptions. It is distinct from planning power to detect a specified effect.
major_error_concepts: Calling any hypothesis-test power calculation a precision calculation without relating it to interval width.
cards.prompt: What is Precision-Based Sample-Size Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Choose n for target estimation precision.
Declare variability and design assumptions.

cards.definition: For a large-population SRS proportion, the normal-approximation planning formula is n approximately z squared times p(1-p) divided by e squared for half-width e. Using p=0.5 maximizes this variance term, not every possible source of survey error.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the formula automatically covers clustering, nonresponse bias, or arbitrary nonprobability selection.
cards.prompt: What is Proportion Sample-Size Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct approximate proportion planning formula.
p=0.5 is conservative for the binomial variance term.

cards.definition: Sample-size inflation for nonresponse divides the required number of completed responses by an assumed response fraction. It budgets invitations or selections but does not remove bias from selective response.
major_error_concepts: Claiming inflating the sample makes nonresponse ignorable.
cards.prompt: What is Nonresponse Allowance in Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Required completions divided by expected response fraction.
More invitations do not eliminate nonresponse bias.

cards.definition: A design effect is the ratio of an estimator's variance under the actual design to a stated reference design, commonly same-size SRS. It is estimator-specific and can reflect clustering, stratification, and weighting.
major_error_concepts: Treating design effect as one universal constant for every variable and estimate.
cards.prompt: What is Design Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Variance ratio relative to an explicit reference design.
Depends on estimator.

cards.definition: A design-effect effective sample size is approximately n/DEFF relative to the chosen SRS comparison. It summarizes precision equivalence, not the literal count of independent respondents or protection against bias.
major_error_concepts: Calling an effective sample size a proof of representativeness.
cards.prompt: What is Effective Sample Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Precision-equivalent sample size relative to stated design.
Does not quantify selection bias.

cards.definition: Power-based sample planning chooses a design and sample size to detect a specified alternative with stated type-I error and power. Effect size, outcome variability, clustering, and allocation affect the calculation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming power is defined without an alternative effect size.
cards.prompt: What is Power-Based Sample Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Plan detection probability for a specified effect and test.

cards.definition: Stratified sampling divides the population into nonoverlapping exhaustive strata and samples within each stratum. It can improve precision or ensure subgroup coverage when allocation and weights reflect the design.
major_error_concepts: Confusing strata sampled throughout the population with selecting only some clusters.
cards.prompt: What is Stratified Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Partition population and sample within each stratum.

cards.definition: If known stratum sizes N_h partition a population of size N, combine stratum mean estimators as Ybar_hat_st=sum_h (N_h/N) Ybar_hat_h. Under SRS within each stratum, Ybar_hat_h is the ordinary stratum sample mean and the combination is design-unbiased. Other within-stratum designs require estimators justified for those designs. Population shares, not sample shares, determine the target population mean; equal stratum weights are appropriate only for equal population sizes or a different explicitly stated target.
major_error_concepts: For any unequal-probability design within strata, the unweighted stratum sample means are automatically design-unbiased, so only the final stratum weights matter.
cards.prompt: Give a stratified estimator of the finite-population mean and state when ordinary within-stratum sample means are justified.
required_concepts: Combine stratum mean estimates using known population shares N_h/N.
Ordinary stratum sample means have the stated unbiasedness under within-stratum SRS, not arbitrary selection.
Distinguish population shares from equal weights or sample shares.

cards.definition: For independent SRS-without-replacement samples in strata h, let W_h=N_h/N and S_h^2=sum_(i in h)(y_i-Ybar_h)^2/(N_h-1), for strata with N_h>1. Then Var(Ybar_hat_st) is the sum of W_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h over noncensus strata; censused strata, including single-unit strata, contribute zero separately. For noncensus strata with n_h>1, replacing S_h^2 by the usual sample variance gives the corresponding unbiased variance estimator. Independence across strata removes cross-covariance terms.
major_error_concepts: Add the unweighted stratum variances and apply one common FPC even when their population shares and sampling fractions differ.
cards.prompt: State the variance of a stratified mean under independent SRS without replacement within strata, and how it is estimated.
required_concepts: Sum W_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h for independent within-stratum SRSWOR.
Each stratum has its own FPC and variance with denominator N_h-1.
Use sample-variance replacement only where it is estimable; census contributions are zero.

cards.definition: Proportional allocation assigns stratum sample sizes proportional to stratum population sizes. With SRS within strata it yields the same sampling fraction across strata, before rounding and other constraints.
major_error_concepts: Calling equal numbers from unequal-sized strata proportional allocation.
cards.prompt: What is Proportional Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: n_h proportional to N_h.

cards.definition: For fixed total sample size and equal per-unit costs, Neyman allocation assigns n_h proportional to N_h S_h to minimize the stratified mean variance under the standard assumptions. More variable strata receive larger sampling fractions.
major_error_concepts: Allocating using variance S_h squared instead of standard deviation in the Neyman formula.
cards.prompt: What is Neyman Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
